title: [HTTP/2] Http2Options.EnablePush defaults to true although every PUSH_PROMISE is refused
body:
## Summary
The client advertises SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH=1 by default, but RejectPushPromiseAsync decodes every pushed field block and answers RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM); push is not implemented anywhere. A server that pushes therefore costs the client a header-block decode and the in-flight pushed bytes for content that is always discarded. A hostile server can also use the open door to make the client decode extra field blocks.

## Location
- `Runtime/Core/Http2Options.cs:10`

## Problem
Http2Options._enablePush defaults to true (Http2Options.cs:10, 35-39) and is serialized as ENABLE_PUSH=1 (Http2Settings.cs:106). RejectPushPromiseAsync then decodes each PUSH_PROMISE field block and answers RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM) (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:1158-1204); the promised id is not recorded in _recentlyResetStreams, so every DATA frame the server already sent on it is debited from the connection window and answered with another RST_STREAM(STREAM_CLOSED) (ReadLoop.cs:203-211). Push is not supported anywhere in the stack.

**Failure scenario.** Against a server that still pushes, every push costs a PUSH_PROMISE block decode, the pushed response bytes already in flight (metered mobile data, connection window) and one or more RST_STREAM frames, for content the client always discards. A hostile server can use the open door to make the client decode arbitrary extra field blocks.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Sections 6.5.2, 8.4

## Suggested fix
Default EnablePush to false (ENABLE_PUSH=0), which turns any PUSH_PROMISE into the connection error already implemented at ReadLoop.cs:1163; keep the option only if push is ever implemented.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Http2Options.EnablePush defaults to false and the initial SETTINGS frame carries ENABLE_PUSH=0.
- [ ] A PUSH_PROMISE received while push is disabled is treated as a connection error (PROTOCOL_ERROR per RFC 9113 section 8.4) and surfaces as UHttpException.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ asserts the default SETTINGS payload and the PUSH_PROMISE reaction; it fails before the fix.

## Context

title: [HTTP/2] Refused pushed streams are not tracked as reset, so each pushed DATA frame triggers another RST_STREAM
body:
## Summary
RejectPushPromiseAsync answers RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM) but does not record the promised stream id in _recentlyResetStreams. DATA frames the server already sent for that id take the unknown-stream branch, are debited from the connection window and each answered with RST_STREAM(STREAM_CLOSED) from the read loop. This wastes downlink on mobile and adds one awaited write per pushed frame.

## Location
- `Runtime/Core/Http2Options.cs:10`

## Problem
Http2Options._enablePush defaults to true (Http2Options.cs:10) and is sent in SETTINGS (Http2Settings.cs:106). RejectPushPromiseAsync always answers RST_STREAM(REFUSED_STREAM) (ReadLoop.cs:1158-1204) but does not call TrackRecentlyResetStream for the promised id, so DATA the server already sent for it takes the unknown-stream branch and writes RST_STREAM(STREAM_CLOSED) per frame from the read loop (ReadLoop.cs:203-211).

**Failure scenario.** A server that still pushes (Link preload based push) sends PUSH_PROMISE plus response headers and up to a window of DATA for every page of assets before the refusal arrives: wasted downlink bytes on mobile and one awaited RST_STREAM write per pushed DATA frame on the read loop.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 8.4

## Suggested fix
Default EnablePush to false (the client cannot use pushes); when it is enabled, track the refused promised id as recently reset.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A refused promised stream id is recorded as recently reset, so late DATA frames on it are discarded without a RST_STREAM per frame (RFC 9113 section 5.1, closed streams).
- [ ] Connection-level flow-control credit for discarded DATA is still returned.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ sends PUSH_PROMISE plus several DATA frames and counts outbound RST_STREAM frames; it fails before the fix.

title: [HTTP/2] Http2Options flow-control surface: zero InitialWindowSize accepted, hidden 1 MiB connection window, test overrides in public class
body:
## Summary
InitialWindowSize accepts 0 and is unbounded above, the connection receive window is a hard-coded 1 MiB constant not derived from any option, and test-only overrides live on the public Http2Options class where setting one flips IsDefault and forces a private transport. Raising InitialWindowSize therefore silently grows per-stream buffers without raising the connection window.

## Location
- `Runtime/Core/Http2Options.cs:75`

## Problem
InitialWindowSize's setter accepts 0..int.MaxValue ('value > int.MaxValue' at Http2Options.cs:80 is always false). Stream WINDOW_UPDATEs are only sent after bytes were consumed (Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:292-324), so a 0 initial window never opens. The connection receive window is not configurable: _connectionRecvWindowTarget = max(65535, min(DefaultConnectionReceiveWindowTargetBytes = 1 MiB, MaxConnectionBufferedBytes)) (Http2Connection.cs:21, 190-192). The per-stream buffer follows the option without an upper bound (Http2Connection.cs:182-186). HTTP/2 tuning is split over two classes (StreamingOptions.Http2StallTimeoutSeconds, DefaultHttp2PerStreamReceiveBufferBytes, MaxConnectionBufferedBytes, ExpectContinueTimeoutMs). Four internal Test*Override properties (Http2Options.cs:26-29) are carried through Clone and IsDefault (lines 238-241, 259-262) and branch production code in the Http2Connection constructor (Http2Connection.cs:182-200) through InternalsVisibleTo.

**Failure scenario.** InitialWindowSize = 0 makes every response with a body hang until the request timeout. InitialWindowSize = 8 MiB (a throughput attempt, #406) is capped in effect by the hard-coded 1 MiB connection window, while the per-stream receive buffer budget silently grows to 8 MiB per stream. Setting a Test override flips IsDefault and forces a private transport.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 6.9

## Suggested fix
Validate InitialWindowSize >= 1 (or a sane minimum) and bound it; expose or derive the connection window from the same option; move the test hooks to an internal options type passed by tests rather than fields of the public class; document which StreamingOptions members are HTTP/2 only.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] InitialWindowSize rejects values below a usable minimum and above a documented bound with ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
- [ ] The connection window is derived from or exposed through the same option set, and the behaviour is documented in XML docs.
- [ ] Test-only overrides move to an internal options type and no longer change IsDefault on the public class.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ covers the validation and the derived connection window; it fails before the fix.

title: [HTTP/2] Http2Options.InitialWindowSize accepts 0, which stalls every response body until the request timeout
body:
## Summary
The setter accepts 0..int.MaxValue and the value is advertised as SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE and used as each stream's receive window. Stream WINDOW_UPDATE is only sent after a chunk is consumed, so a zero window never opens. Any response with a body then hangs until request.Timeout.

## Location
- `Runtime/Core/Http2Options.cs:80`

## Problem
The setter accepts 0..int.MaxValue (Runtime/Core/Http2Options.cs:75-84) and the value is advertised as SETTINGS_INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE and used as each stream's receive window (Http2Settings.cs:108, Http2Connection.cs:362-363). Stream-level WINDOW_UPDATE is only ever sent after a chunk was consumed (OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync, Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:292-324) or for padding-only frames (ReadLoop.cs:299-305); there is no path that opens a zero window.

**Failure scenario.** InitialWindowSize = 0 (a valid value per the option and the RFC): the server may send HEADERS but no DATA byte, the client never sends a stream WINDOW_UPDATE because nothing is consumed, and every response with a body hangs until request.Timeout.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Sections 6.9.1, 6.9.2

## Suggested fix
Reject values below a usable minimum in the setter (e.g. < 1, or below 16384 with a clear message), or send an initial stream WINDOW_UPDATE when a response starts with a zero window.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] InitialWindowSize setter rejects 0 and values below a documented minimum with ArgumentOutOfRangeException and a clear message.
- [ ] No configuration path leaves a response stream with a zero receive window and no way to open it.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix.

title: [HTTP/2] Http2Options.MaxHeaderListSize above 256 KB is advertised but not honoured, and the breach is connection-fatal
body:
## Summary
Three independent limits apply to response headers: MaxHeaderListSize (advertised, per-stream error), MaxDecodedHeaderBytes (decoder cap, default 256 KB, GOAWAY COMPRESSION_ERROR) and a hard-coded 256 KB header block ceiling (ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM). Raising MaxHeaderListSize tells the server larger lists are acceptable, yet a 300 KB list kills the whole connection instead of one stream.

## Location
- `Runtime/Core/Http2Options.cs:106`

## Problem
MaxHeaderListSize (Http2Options.cs:101-114, any value > 0) is sent as SETTINGS_MAX_HEADER_LIST_SIZE and enforced per stream in ApplyDecodedHeaders (ReadLoop.cs:610-621, stream error). Independently MaxDecodedHeaderBytes (Http2Options.cs:116-129, default 256 KB) caps the decoder (HpackDecoder.cs:132-140, HpackDecodingException -> GOAWAY COMPRESSION_ERROR, ReadLoop.cs:94-106), and the hard-coded MaxHeaderBlockBytesCeiling = 256 KB (Http2Connection.cs:110) caps a multi-frame encoded block (HeaderBlockByteLimit, ReadLoop.cs:566-573, ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM connection error). No setter cross-validates them.

**Failure scenario.** options.Http2.MaxHeaderListSize = 1 MiB tells the server 1 MiB of headers is acceptable; a 300 KB response header list then fails every stream on the connection with COMPRESSION_ERROR (decoder cap) or ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM (block ceiling) instead of being accepted, or at worst rejected for that one stream.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Sections 6.5.2, 10.5.1

## Suggested fix
Derive the decoder cap and the block ceiling from MaxHeaderListSize (one public knob), or clamp/validate MaxHeaderListSize against them at construction, so the advertised limit is the enforced one and an oversized list is a stream error.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The advertised MaxHeaderListSize is the enforced limit: decoder cap and block ceiling are derived from it or validated against it at construction.
- [ ] An oversized header list produces a stream-level error, not a connection error, where RFC 9113 section 6.5.2 permits it.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ with a header list between 256 KB and the configured limit; it fails before the fix.

title: [HTTP/2] HpackHuffman and HpackStaticTable use ValueTuple arrays and a 513-object tree instead of blob-initialised primitive tables
body:
## Summary
The Huffman encode table and the static table are tuple arrays filled element by element in type initialisers, and the decode tree is built at first use as 513 heap objects walked bit by bit. This adds initialiser code to every build and about 20 KB of long-lived allocations on the first HTTP/2 header block.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/HpackHuffman.cs:13`

## Problem
HpackHuffman.s_encodeTable is a (uint Code, byte BitLength)[] with 256 literal elements (HpackHuffman.cs:13-271) and HpackStaticTable.s_table a (string,string)[] with 62 elements (HpackStaticTable.cs:20-84). C# cannot emit ValueTuple arrays as RVA data, so both are filled element by element inside the type initialisers. The static constructor (HpackHuffman.cs:287-299) then builds the decode tree with InsertIntoTree: one HuffmanNode object per tree node (257 leaves -> 513 nodes, each with two references and an int), walked bit by bit in Decode (lines 386-413). HpackIntegerCodec/Huffman are only initialised on first HPACK use, so nothing runs at startup.

**Failure scenario.** Every build carries a type initialiser with ~260 struct stores for the Huffman table, and the first HTTP/2 header block allocates ~513 small objects (about 20 KB on 64-bit) that live for the process lifetime and are pointer-chased one bit at a time on every Huffman-coded header string.

## Spec reference
RFC 7541 Appendix B

## Suggested fix
Store the codes as static readonly uint[] and byte[] (or ReadOnlySpan<byte> over a constant blob), which compile to RVA data with no initialiser code, and decode with a flat int[]/ushort[] state table (4- or 8-bit steps) instead of a node tree.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Huffman codes and lengths are stored as static readonly primitive arrays or ReadOnlySpan blobs that compile to RVA data.
- [ ] Decoding uses a flat table-driven state machine with no per-node objects.
- [ ] First HTTP/2 header block performs no table-building allocations, measured and recorded.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ with RFC 7541 vectors passes before and after (behaviour parity) and an allocation assertion fails before.

title: [HTTP/2] HpackHuffman table codes '{' as 0x7fffe/19 bits instead of 0x7ffe/15, breaking decode and encode against conformant peers
body:
## Summary
Entry 123 in the Huffman table is (0x7fffe, 19) where RFC 7541 Appendix B specifies 0x7ffe with 15 bits. The code is incomplete and its prefix collides with other symbols, so a conformant peer sending '{' in a Huffman-coded header (for example report-to or nel JSON) makes the client throw and send GOAWAY(COMPRESSION_ERROR), and requests with '{' in a value are mis-encoded. Origins sending such headers are unreachable over HTTP/2.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/HpackHuffman.cs:138`

## Problem
HpackHuffman.cs:138 has `(0x7fffe, 19), // (123) '{'`; RFC 7541 Appendix B gives '{' (123) = 7ffe [15]. Verified numerically from the file: the Kraft sum of the 257 code lengths is 524273/524288 (not 1, so the code is incomplete) and becomes exactly 1 with 15 bits; the 19-bit code 1111111111111111110 is a prefix of the 23-bit codes of symbols 147,149,150,151,152,155,157,158,165,166,168,174,175,180,182,183 (0x7fffe0-0x7fffef). Decode side: InsertIntoTree (HpackHuffman.cs:302-320) marks an interior node as leaf 123, and no code has the RFC prefix `14 ones + 0`, so Decode hits `next == null` (HpackHuffman.cs:405-406) and throws HpackDecodingException; ReadLoopAsync maps that to GOAWAY(COMPRESSION_ERROR) + FailAllStreams (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:94-106). The comment at HpackHuffman.cs:403 ('The HPACK code is complete, so this is unreachable') is false for this table. Encode side: EncodeCore (HpackHuffman.cs:347-374) emits the 19-bit code whenever HpackEncoder.EncodeString picks Huffman (HpackEncoder.cs:187-199). Present since the first implementation (git 87dcfe1). Tests: HpackHuffmanTests.RoundTrip_PrintableAsciiValues (Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/HpackHuffmanTests.cs:34) round-trips 32..126 through the same wrong table so it passes; the RFC vectors used contain no '{'; no test decodes bytes >= 0x80.

**Failure scenario.** A server Huffman-encodes any response field containing '{' per the RFC (e.g. Cloudflare/Google `report-to: {"endpoints":[...` or `nel: {"report_to":...`, JSON in set-cookie or custom headers): the client throws on the 15-bit code, sends GOAWAY(COMPRESSION_ERROR) and fails every stream on the connection; an idempotent request is replayed once on a fresh connection and fails the same way, so the origin is unreachable over HTTP/2. Conversely a request header value such as `x-meta: {abcdefghijklmnop}` (Huffman shorter than raw) is sent with an 18-ones+0 code; a conformant server decodes a byte from the 0x93..0xB7 group plus misaligned garbage (corrupted value) or answers COMPRESSION_ERROR. Response values containing the 16 listed high bytes (UTF-8 continuation bytes) are also mis-decoded as '{' plus garbage.

## Spec reference
RFC 7541 Appendix B, Section 5.2

## Suggested fix
Change entry 123 to (0x7ffe, 15). Add a table self-check test (Kraft sum == 1, prefix-free) and decode/encode vectors produced by an independent implementation covering all 256 symbols, not a self round-trip.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Entry 123 is (0x7ffe, 15) and the code table is complete and prefix-free (Kraft sum equals 1).
- [ ] Decoding RFC 7541 vectors for all 256 symbols produced by an independent implementation succeeds, and encoding matches them byte for byte.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ checks the Kraft sum, prefix-freeness and a header containing '{' decoded from conformant bytes; it fails before the fix.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-protocol-01` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: critical. Angle: rfc-compat.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Re-derived from the file, not the reviewer's text. HpackHuffman.cs:138 is `(0x7fffe, 19), // (123) '{'`; RFC 7541 Appendix B gives 7ffe [15]. A script over the 256 table entries plus EOS (0x3fffffff/30) gives a Kraft sum of 524273/524288 (an RFC-complete code sums to 1; the deficit 15/2^19 is exactly 2^-15 - 2^-19, i.e. one 15-bit code written as 19 bits), and the 19-bit code is a prefix of the 23-bit codes of symbols 147,149,150,151,152,155,157,158,165,166,168,174,175,180,182,183. No table entry starts with or is a prefix of the RFC code 111111111111110, so Decode walks to a null child and throws (HpackHuffman.cs:405-406; the 'code is complete, unreachable' comment at 403 is false). HpackDecoder.cs:293-295 calls it for every Huffman string; ReadLoop.cs:94-106 turns the exception into GOAWAY(COMPRESSION_ERROR)+FailAllStreams. Encode side: HpackEncoder.cs:187-199 uses Huffman whenever shorter and EncodeCore (HpackHuffman.cs:347-374) emits the wrong 19-bit code. No refuting test: HpackHuffmanTests.cs:34-41 round-trips 32..126 through the same table, the RFC C.4 vectors contain no '{', nothing decodes independent vectors; the fuzz seeds are the same C.3/C.4 vectors. Any conformant peer that Huffman-codes a field containing '{' (report-to / nel JSON values are the common case) kills the connection, and the idempotent replay fails the same way.

title: [HTTP/2] HPACK allocates per header: Huffman decode writer, byte[] copy, string, list nodes and boxed enumerator
body:
## Summary
Huffman decoding creates a pooled writer, appends byte by byte, copies to a byte[] and then builds a string; the dynamic table allocates a LinkedListNode per entry; Encode boxes a List enumerator and rents several pool buffers per string. A response with 15 Huffman-coded headers costs about 45 avoidable allocations on the read loop.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/HpackHuffman.cs:386`

## Problem
HpackHuffman.Decode allocates a PooledArrayBufferWriter per string, appends one byte per GetSpan/Advance call, walks HuffmanNode objects one bit at a time and returns WrittenMemory.ToArray() (HpackHuffman.cs:384-437); HpackDecoder.DecodeString then builds the string from that array (HpackDecoder.cs:293-297). HpackDynamicTable.Add allocates a LinkedListNode per entry and recomputes Latin-1 byte counts on every add and eviction (HpackDynamicTable.cs:31-63). HpackEncoder.Encode enumerates IReadOnlyList through the interface (boxed List enumerator, HpackEncoder.cs:66) and EncodeString rents two pooled buffers and makes three passes per string (HpackEncoder.cs:174-215).

**Failure scenario.** A response with 15 Huffman-coded header strings costs about 45 avoidable allocations and a pointer-chasing decode on the read loop; a request adds a boxed enumerator, list nodes and about 30 pool rents under _writeLock.

## Suggested fix
Decode Huffman into a rented or stack buffer with a table-driven (nibble or byte) decoder and create the string directly; back the dynamic table with a ring buffer that stores entry sizes; iterate the header list by index and encode strings straight into the output writer.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Huffman decode writes into a rented or stack buffer and creates the string directly, without an intermediate byte[].
- [ ] The dynamic table is backed by a ring buffer storing entry sizes; encode iterates headers by index.
- [ ] Allocations per decoded header block drop to the target recorded in the PR (strings only), measured with an allocation test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/.

title: [HTTP/2] Stream admission reads ConcurrentDictionary.Count repeatedly while holding _streamCreateLock and _writeLock
body:
## Summary
FreeStreamSlotsLocked, HasFreeStreamSlot, the admission pump and DispatchAsync read _activeStreams.Count, which takes every bucket lock, up to three times per request under the connection's two hottest locks. Under many concurrent requests this contends with stream removal and lengthens the write lock hold.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Admission.cs:72`

## Problem
FreeStreamSlotsLocked reads _activeStreams.Count (Admission.cs:72) in AcquireStreamSlotAsync, HasFreeStreamSlot and every PumpAdmissionWaitersLocked; DispatchAsync reads it again under both locks (Http2Connection.cs:351). ConcurrentDictionary.Count takes every bucket lock of the dictionary. TrackRecentlyResetStream does the same on _recentlyResetStreams for every reset (Lifecycle.cs:256).

**Failure scenario.** With many concurrent requests each dispatch acquires all dictionary locks several times inside the connection's two hottest locks, contending with stream removal on other threads and lengthening the _writeLock hold for every request.

## Suggested fix
Keep an Interlocked open-stream counter updated where streams are added and removed (the code already centralises removal in RemoveActiveStream/TryRemoveActiveStream) and use it for admission and drain checks.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] An Interlocked open-stream counter is maintained where streams are added and removed and used for admission and drain checks.
- [ ] The counter stays consistent on all removal paths (completion, reset, cancellation, connection failure).
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ covers admission at MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS and the counter after resets and failures.

title: [HTTP/2] Per-request and per-control-frame allocations on the HTTP/2 hot path: manager keys, frame-payload closures, lower-cased header names
body:
## Summary
Http2ConnectionManager formats a key string per request, every WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM, PING and GOAWAY allocates a closure and delegate through SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync, and mixed-case header names are lower-cased into new strings under _writeLock. These show as GC Alloc per request.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:88`

## Problem
Http2ConnectionManager builds the lookup key with string interpolation on every request (boxed port plus a new string, Http2ConnectionManager.cs:62, 76, 233; four-argument format with an object[] for tunnels, 497). SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync takes an Action<byte[]> that captures its arguments, so every WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM, PING and GOAWAY allocates a closure and a delegate (Lifecycle.cs:34-86, Liveness.cs:244-255). DispatchAsync lower-cases each mixed-case header name into a new string under _writeLock (Http2Connection.cs:399, 615-637), wraps the completion await in an extra async method (577-585) and registers a capturing lambda per queued admission (Admission.cs:118, against the ct.Register rule in platform.md).

**Failure scenario.** Each request allocates a key string, a boxed int and one string per canonical-case header; each consumed DATA frame adds a closure and delegate through the window update; visible as GC Alloc per request in the profiler and extra work inside the write lock.

## Suggested fix
Cache the manager key per origin (or key on a struct), write the 4/8-byte payloads from arguments passed as state (static lambda or a small switch), cache lower-cased names for common headers, await the stream's ValueTask directly and use a static callback with a state object for the admission registration.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The manager key is cached per origin or replaced by a struct key; no string formatting per request.
- [ ] Control frame payloads are written without closure or delegate allocation.
- [ ] Common header names are lower-cased from a cache.
- [ ] Allocations per HTTP/2 request are measured before and after, with an allocation-gate test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/.

title: [HTTP/2] Read loop awaits _writeLock for control frames, so a DATA write blocked by TCP back-pressure stalls inbound processing until the 60 s stall timer
body:
## Summary
The read loop writes SETTINGS ACK, PING ACK, WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM inline by awaiting _writeLock, which an uploader holds for the whole socket write of a DATA frame. If that write blocks, nothing is read, including the WINDOW_UPDATE the upload needs. Both sides can wait until the 60 s stall timeout fails the connection and every stream on it. Marked plausible by the reviewer.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:101`

## Problem
The read loop awaits the write lock inline for SETTINGS ACK (ReadLoop.cs:899), PING ACK (ReadLoop.cs:944), connection and stream WINDOW_UPDATE (ReadLoop.cs:207, 304, 307 -> Lifecycle.cs:389, 101) and RST_STREAM (ReadLoop.cs:210, 415). An uploader holds the same lock for the whole socket write of a DATA frame (Send.cs:189-241), which is finished with the connection token only. While the read loop waits, no frame is read: no WINDOW_UPDATE for uploads, no PING ACK, no response data. The only bound is FailConnectionIfSendStalled after Http2StallTimeoutSeconds = 60 (Lifecycle.cs:499-511), which fails every stream on the connection. The inline wait gives natural back-pressure against PING/SETTINGS floods, so a fix has to keep a bound.

**Failure scenario.** Large upload and large download run on one connection against a server whose frame loop awaits its own flushes (Kestrel-style output back-pressure). A transient makes the client's DATA write block; the read loop then needs the lock for a connection WINDOW_UPDATE and stops reading; the server's output fills, its loop blocks on a flush and stops reading the client's DATA. Both sides wait until the client's 60 s stall timer fails the connection and all its streams. Confirm with a bidirectional soak against Kestrel with small socket buffers.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 10.5

## Suggested fix
Never block the read loop on the write lock: put control frames (ACKs, WINDOW_UPDATE, RST_STREAM) into a small bounded outbound queue that the current or next lock holder drains, with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM/connection failure when the bound is exceeded.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The read loop never awaits the write lock: control frames go into a small bounded outbound queue drained by the current or next lock holder.
- [ ] Exceeding the queue bound fails the connection with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ with a blocked write and an incoming PING shows reads continue; it fails before the fix.
- [ ] Bidirectional soak against Kestrel with small socket buffers recorded in the PR.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-14` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: concurrency.

Verification: Plausible: the code is as described; the outcome depends on runtime, device or peer behaviour that a static review cannot settle.

Verifier note: Structure confirmed: the read loop awaits _writeLock inline for SETTINGS ACK (ReadLoop.cs:899), PING ACK (ReadLoop.cs:944), WINDOW_UPDATE (ReadLoop.cs:207, 223, 304, 307 -> Lifecycle.cs:364-389 -> 101) and RST_STREAM (ReadLoop.cs:86, 210, 229 -> Lifecycle.cs:72-85 -> 101), and an uploader holds the same lock across the whole socket write of a DATA frame (Send.cs:189-241, WriteFrameLockedAsync with the connection token only, Send.cs:75-92). While the read loop waits, ReadFrameLeaseAsync is not called, so nothing inbound is processed; the only bound is FailConnectionIfSendStalled (Lifecycle.cs:499-511). No queue or try-lock path exists. The full mutual stall needs a peer that stops reading while its own writes are blocked and enough pending output to fill the client's TCP receive buffer, which depends on the server implementation and socket buffer sizes; with event-driven servers the effect is only that inbound processing is delayed by each blocked DATA write. Not settled statically.

title: [HTTP/2] SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync swallows cancellation, so a cancelled body read permanently loses a stream WINDOW_UPDATE
body:
## Summary
SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync catches OperationCanceledException and returns normally, so OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync never runs its compensation that withdraws the local window credit. After a cancelled read the bytes are still returned and credited, but no WINDOW_UPDATE is sent, leaving the peer's stream window permanently short. After a few such losses with the default 65535 window the server can send nothing and the download hangs.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:116`

## Problem
SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync waits for _writeLock with the caller token (Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:101) and catches OperationCanceledException when either that token or the connection token is cancelled, and ObjectDisposedException, returning normally (lines 116-123). OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync credits the local stream receive window first (line 304), calls SendWindowUpdateAsync with the consumer's read token (line 307) and withdraws the credit only in catch blocks for exactly those two exception types (lines 309-318), which therefore never run; the comment at lines 300-303 ('Withdrawn again when the frame was not sent') is not true. The token is the caller's ReadAsync token (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:200-203, 402-415). AbortStreamFromBodySourceAsync and SendCancelRstAfterRequestCancellationAsync carry the same dead catch clauses (Lifecycle.cs:230-235, 341-346). No test references the withdrawal path.

**Failure scenario.** A consumer reads a streamed HTTP/2 body with cancellable reads and keeps reading after one is cancelled (pause/resume, per-read timeouts). If the token fires between the read's entry check and the WINDOW_UPDATE acquiring _writeLock (immediately when already cancelled, or while the lock is held by another stream's DATA write on a slow uplink), ReadAsync still returns the bytes, the local window is credited, and no WINDOW_UPDATE is sent. The peer's stream window is permanently short by that chunk (up to 16 KB); after about four such losses with the default 65,535 window the server can send nothing more, nothing is buffered so the stall detector does not fire (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:388-400), and a handed-off streamed response has no request deadline: the download hangs.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 6.9

## Suggested fix
Make the helper's contract explicit: let it report 'not sent' (bool result or rethrow) and have OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync withdraw the credit on that result; better, send the stream WINDOW_UPDATE under the connection token only (it is connection bookkeeping, not part of the caller's read) so a cancelled read cannot drop it. Remove the unreachable catch clauses.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A WINDOW_UPDATE caused by a consumed chunk is sent under the connection token only, so a cancelled read cannot drop it.
- [ ] The helper reports not-sent explicitly (or rethrows) and the unreachable catch clauses are removed.
- [ ] Deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ cancels the read token while the write lock is held and asserts the WINDOW_UPDATE is still sent; it fails before the fix.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-design-16` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: code-smell.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. ReadAsync copies the bytes, then CompleteDetachedChunkAsync passes the caller's read token to OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:200-206, 402-415), which credits the local stream window (Lifecycle.cs:304) and calls SendWindowUpdateAsync(…, ct) (307). SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync waits for _writeLock with that token (101) and swallows OperationCanceledException when ct or _cts is cancelled, and every ObjectDisposedException (116-123), returning normally. So the withdrawal catches at 309-318 cannot run for those cases (an OCE that fails the inner filter also fails the identical outer filter and lands in the generic catch at 319), the comment at 300-303 is false, and a token that fires between the entry check (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:193) and the lock acquisition drops the WINDOW_UPDATE while ReadAsync still returns the bytes: the peer's stream window stays short by that chunk for good. The stall detector does not cover it because nothing is buffered (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:388-400). Needs a caller that keeps reading after a token it passed was cancelled (per-read timeouts), and the window is narrow unless _writeLock is contended, so an edge case. One inaccuracy: the ObjectDisposedException catches in AbortStreamFromBodySourceAsync and SendCancelRstAfterRequestCancellationAsync are reachable, because SendRstStreamAsync evaluates _cts.Token (Lifecycle.cs:78), which throws once _cts is disposed (Lifecycle.cs:651).

Related: [[R11-http2-runtime-14]].

title: [HTTP/2] Http2ResponseBodySource uses its Http2Stream without a lease after a concurrent Abort released it
body:
## Summary
Http2ResponseBodySource keeps calling OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync with its Http2Stream reference after Abort from the stall scanner has released the body source's lifetime reference. The stream object can already be pooled and re-rented by a new request on the same connection. The old reader then credits and advertises window for the new request's stream, over-crediting it.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:297`

## Problem
CleanupAsync releases the body source's stream reference (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:461-464), after which the stream can be pooled and re-rented (LIFO pool). A ReadAsync running concurrently with that Abort (the maintenance thread calls Abort on live readers, Lifecycle.cs:482) still calls OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync(_stream, ...) (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:413), which reads stream.StreamId, credits stream.AdjustRecvWindowSize and sends WINDOW_UPDATE for that id with no TryAcquireLease (Lifecycle.cs:297-307). Abort/DrainAsync/DisposeAsync also read _stream.StreamId after cleanup (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:242, 248, 278). Every other holder of a looked-up stream uses TryAcquireLease.

**Failure scenario.** The stall scanner aborts a body at the moment its reader resumes (for example after an app resume); the stream object is re-rented by a new request on the same connection before the reader reaches line 304, and the old reader credits and advertises window for the new request's stream, over-crediting it by one chunk.

## Suggested fix
Capture the stream id in the body source at construction and take a lease (TryAcquireLease(id, connection)) in OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync before touching the stream.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync takes a lease on the stream id captured at construction (TryAcquireLease(id, connection)) before touching the stream and does nothing if the lease fails
- [ ] A reader that resumes after Abort never credits or sends WINDOW_UPDATE for a re-rented stream
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] Stream WINDOW_UPDATE is dropped when the reader's token is cancelled while the local window credit is kept
body:
## Summary
Http2ResponseBodySource.ReadAsync completes a chunk with the reader's CancellationToken, and OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync credits the local receive window before sending WINDOW_UPDATE with that same token. If the token fires or the write lock is held, the update is never sent but the credit stays, so the peer's stream window shrinks permanently. After a few such events the server has no window left and the download stalls.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:307`

## Problem
Http2ResponseBodySource.ReadAsync copies the bytes, then awaits CompleteDetachedChunkAsync(chunk, ct) with the reader's token (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:200-203, 413). OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync credits the receive window (Lifecycle.cs:304) and calls SendWindowUpdateAsync(streamId, len, ct); SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync gates the lock with that token (Lifecycle.cs:101) and swallows the OperationCanceledException (Lifecycle.cs:116-119), so the catch blocks at Lifecycle.cs:309-318 that would withdraw the credit are dead code. SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync returns cancelled for an already-cancelled token even when the lock is free. ReadAsync still returns the bytes, so the caller sees a successful read. Cancelling one read and reading on is a supported pattern (Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2BodyReadCancellationTests.cs asserts it for a pending read on an empty queue; no test covers cancellation during the window update).

**Failure scenario.** A consumer uses a per-read timeout token. A token fires while its chunk is being completed (or while _writeLock is held by an upload): the 16 KB credit is never advertised. After four such events on a default 65535-byte window the server has no window left, nothing is buffered locally, the stall scanner does not fire (it needs buffered bytes) and the body read waits forever.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 6.9

## Suggested fix
Do not gate the WINDOW_UPDATE on the reader's token: use the connection token (or CancellationToken.None) for the lock wait, or accumulate unsent credit on the stream and flush it with the next update.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The stream WINDOW_UPDATE is sent with the connection token (or CancellationToken.None for the lock wait), or unsent credit is accumulated on the stream and flushed with the next update
- [ ] A cancelled per-read token never leaves the peer's advertised stream window smaller than the local credited window
- [ ] A download whose reads are repeatedly cancelled continues to receive data beyond the initial 65535-byte window
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-04` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: concurrency.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: ReadAsync copies the bytes and then awaits CompleteDetachedChunkAsync(chunk, ct) with the reader's token (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:200-203, 413). OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync credits the local window (Lifecycle.cs:304) and calls SendWindowUpdateAsync(..., ct); SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync waits on _writeLock with that token (Lifecycle.cs:101) and swallows the resulting OCE itself (116-119), so the withdraw-credit catch at 309-313 can never run for a reader-token cancellation: the frame is not sent, the credit stays, ReadAsync returns the bytes as a success. The peer's view of the stream window shrinks by the chunk's flow-controlled length for good; once it reaches 0 nothing is buffered locally, IsStalled needs buffered bytes (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:388-399), a handed-off streaming body has no request deadline, so the read waits forever. Trigger window: the token must fire between the ThrowIfCancellationRequested at the top of ReadAsync and the lock grant, i.e. while _writeLock is held by another writer (a large DATA write on a slow link) or in a very short synchronous window, and the consumer must keep reading afterwards; Http2BodyReadCancellationTests shows read-on-after-cancel is supported. Rare per read, permanent per hit.

title: [HTTP/2] Idle connections keep a 5 s maintenance timer and 30 s keep-alive timer that allocate on every tick
body:
## Summary
MaintenanceLoopAsync and KeepAliveLoopAsync run for the whole life of every HTTP/2 connection, even with no open streams. Each maintenance tick enumerates two ConcurrentDictionary instances, which allocates enumerators, and reads the clock. An application with several idle HTTP/2 origins sees periodic GC allocations and timer wake-ups with nothing in flight.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:454`

## Problem
MaintenanceLoopAsync awaits Task.Delay(_maintenanceInterval) forever (Lifecycle.cs:448-467) and each tick enumerates two ConcurrentDictionary instances (allocating enumerators, Lifecycle.cs:473, 521) and reads the clock, whether or not streams exist. KeepAliveLoopAsync wakes every PingInterval only to find no streams (Liveness.cs:46-50, 75). Each Task.Delay allocates a timer, a promise and a cancellation registration. Connections are never closed for idleness (finding 12), so the timers run for the session.

**Failure scenario.** A game with five idle HTTP/2 origins sees a steady trickle of managed allocations and timer wake-ups from the HTTP client while nothing is in flight, visible in the Unity profiler as periodic GC Alloc and contributing to Boehm GC pressure.

## Suggested fix
Arm the maintenance and keep-alive timers only while streams are open or recently reset entries exist (start on first stream, stop when the connection goes idle), or use one shared System.Threading.Timer per manager with allocation-free scans.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Maintenance and keep-alive timers are armed only while streams are open or recently reset entries exist, or one shared timer per manager is used
- [ ] An idle connection with no streams performs zero managed allocations per maintenance interval, measured in a test
- [ ] Stall scanning, recently-reset pruning and keep-alive PING behaviour for connections with open streams are unchanged
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] Transport-initiated stall abort surfaces to the body reader as ObjectDisposedException instead of UHttpException
body:
## Summary
When the stall scanner aborts a response body whose buffered bytes were not consumed for Http2StallTimeoutSeconds, Abort sets the terminal state and disposes the source. A resumed ReadAsync then throws ObjectDisposedException, which looks like the caller's own use-after-dispose bug and carries no UHttpErrorType. Callers cannot distinguish a stall abort from a programming error or react to it.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:482`

## Problem
ScanForStalledStreams calls stream.ResponseBodySource?.Abort() when buffered bytes were not consumed for StreamingOptions.Http2StallTimeoutSeconds (Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:469-489; IsStalled at Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:388-400). Abort -> BeginCleanup sets the terminal state to Aborted and _disposed = 1 (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:246-249, 417-438) and CleanupAsync completes the queue with ObjectDisposedException (lines 444-449). The reader's next ReadAsync therefore throws ObjectDisposedException('Http2ResponseBodySource') from ThrowIfDisposed (lines 192, 517-521); the same goes for DrainAsync and GetTrailersAsync. Other transport-side terminations go through Fault with a UHttpException (per-stream buffer full, size cap, malformed response, connection failure). The only stall test (Http2ConnectionTests.StreamingResponses.cs:578-620) asserts the RST_STREAM and never reads the body afterwards.

**Failure scenario.** A game pauses consumption of a streamed download for longer than 60 s (loading screen, app in background) while data is buffered. When it resumes, ReadAsync throws ObjectDisposedException, which looks like the caller's own use-after-dispose bug, is not a UHttpException, carries no UHttpErrorType, and is not seen as retryable by the retry logic or by handlers that catch UHttpException (CLAUDE.md section 3 error model).

## Suggested fix
Give the stall path its own terminal outcome: fault the body with UHttpException(UHttpErrorType.Timeout or NetworkError, 'response body not read for N s') before releasing buffers and sending RST_STREAM, and keep ObjectDisposedException for reads after the caller's own Dispose. Assert the reader-visible error in the stall test.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A stall abort faults the body with UHttpException of type Timeout or NetworkError and a message naming the stall duration, before buffers are released and RST_STREAM is sent
- [ ] ObjectDisposedException is thrown only for reads after the caller's own Dispose
- [ ] The stall test asserts the reader-visible UHttpException type
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-design-17` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: code-smell.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. ScanForStalledStreams calls ResponseBodySource.Abort() for a stream whose buffered bytes were not consumed for the stall timeout (Lifecycle.cs:469-489; IsStalled at Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:388-400). Abort -> BeginCleanup sets TerminalStateAborted and _disposed = 1 (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:246-249, 417-438); CleanupAsync completes the queue and faults trailers with ObjectDisposedException (444-456). The reader's next ReadAsync/DrainAsync/GetTrailersAsync throws ObjectDisposedException from ThrowIfDisposed (192, 232, 253, 517-521). Nothing above maps it: UHttpStreamingResponse.ReadBodyAsync and ResponseBodyStream forward the body source call directly (UHttpStreamingResponse.cs:59-62, ResponseBodyStream.cs:150). Other transport-side terminations use Fault with a UHttpException (ReadLoop.cs:265, 313, 383). The only stall test asserts the RST_STREAM and never reads afterwards (Http2ConnectionTests.StreamingResponses.cs:578-620). This contradicts the error model in CLAUDE.md section 3 for a transport-initiated abort; it needs a consumer that pauses reading for the stall timeout (60 s default) with data buffered.

Also reported as `http2-runtime-18` (merged into this issue).

title: [HTTP/2] FinalizeResourceDispose returns the HPACK encoder's pooled buffer while a dispatch can still call Encode under _writeLock
body:
## Summary
FinalizeResourceDispose disposes the HPACK encoder once the read loop, keep-alive and maintenance tasks have ended, without waiting for writers. A DispatchAsync that passed AcceptsNewStreamsCore before shutdown and holds _writeLock can still call Encode afterwards. Encode then re-rents a pooled buffer that is never returned, or uses a buffer another owner already holds.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:661`

## Problem
FinalizeResourceDispose runs once the read loop, keep-alive and maintenance tasks ended (Lifecycle.cs:600-607, 641-662) and disposes _hpackEncoder, but it does not wait for writers: _writeLock is deliberately left alone (653-658). A DispatchAsync that passed AcceptsNewStreamsCore before _cts was cancelled continues to build headers and call _hpackEncoder.Encode (Http2Connection.cs:345-410). PooledArrayBufferWriter.Reset after Dispose rents a new buffer (PooledArrayBufferWriter.cs:179-189) that nothing returns; a Dispose concurrent with Encode nulls _buffer under the non-thread-safe writer.

**Failure scenario.** A connection is disposed (GOAWAY drain, PING timeout) while a request holds the write lock between the accept check and Encode and is descheduled long enough for the shutdown tasks to finish: Encode re-rents a buffer that is never returned (ByteArrayPool ActiveCount drifts, the #292 leak oracle) or throws InvalidOperationException/NullReferenceException that surfaces as the request's error.

## Suggested fix
Dispose the encoder under the write lock (take _writeLock in the finalizer path, or mark the encoder closed and let the last lock holder return the buffer), and make Encode fail with a mapped connection-closed error after disposal instead of re-renting.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The encoder is disposed under _writeLock, or marked closed so the last lock holder returns its buffer
- [ ] Encode after disposal fails with a mapped connection-closed UHttpException and rents no buffer
- [ ] ByteArrayPool ActiveCount returns to its baseline after disposing a connection while a dispatch is mid-flight
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] Http2Connection.Dispose writes GOAWAY synchronously although its comments say Dispose must never block
body:
## Summary
SendGoAwayOnDisposeBestEffort calls _stream.Write twice and _stream.Flush synchronously after _writeLock.Wait(0). On a half-open connection with a full send buffer these writes block the disposing thread until the OS gives up. On the Unity main thread that freezes a frame or hangs on quit.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:700`

## Problem
SendGoAwayOnDisposeBestEffort calls _stream.Write twice and _stream.Flush synchronously (Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:700-702) after _writeLock.Wait(0), with the comments 'Use synchronous writes in Dispose to avoid async context deadlocks' and 'Dispose must never block or throw' (lines 688, 706, 715). _writeLock only proves that no other frame writer is active, not that the socket is writable; no send timeout is set anywhere in Runtime/Transport. For the Saea and PollSelect socket modes Stream.Write is sync-over-async (SaeaStream.cs:91-92, PollSelectStream.cs:86-87: WriteAsync(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult()). Dispose runs on whatever thread disposes the client (typically the Unity main thread via RawSocketTransport.Dispose -> Http2ConnectionManager.Dispose) and inline on the read loop (TryCompleteDrain(inline: true), ReadLoop.cs:1014).

**Failure scenario.** On a half-open connection whose send buffer is full (network lost with unacknowledged data queued), the GOAWAY write blocks the disposing thread until the OS gives up on the connection; on the main thread that is a frozen frame or a hang on quit. Whether the buffer is full at that instant depends on the network state, so this needs a device/lossy-network run to confirm.

## Suggested fix
Skip the GOAWAY on Dispose unless it can be queued without blocking (hand it to a bounded background write owned by the connection, with the stall bound that already exists), or drop it: closing the TLS stream is a sufficient signal for a client.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Dispose never performs a blocking network write: the GOAWAY is either queued to a bounded background write owned by the connection or dropped
- [ ] Disposing a connection whose stream blocks on write returns within a bounded time in a test using a blocking stream
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] Connection that fails in the read loop or on a frame write sends GOAWAY but never closes the transport stream
body:
## Summary
The ReadLoopAsync catch blocks and FailConnectionAfterWriteError send GOAWAY and call FailAllStreams, which only cancels _cts and fails streams. Nothing disposes the connection, so the socket and TLS state stay open until a later request for the same origin evicts it, or forever for a GOAWAY-drained connection. Each affected origin keeps a lingering half-open socket and server-side resources.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:107`

## Problem
ReadLoopAsync's catch blocks (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:94-120) send GOAWAY and call FailAllStreams, which only cancels _cts and fails streams (Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:549-581); nothing calls Dispose/DisposeStreamOnce. Same for write failures (FailConnectionAfterWriteError, Http2Connection.Send.cs:94-107) and peer EOF without GOAWAY (IOException from Http2FrameCodec.ReadExactAsync:262 -> generic catch). Only the PING-timeout, send-stall and drain-complete paths call Dispose (Liveness.cs:223-224, Lifecycle.cs:508-509, Admission.cs:211-214). FailAllStreams removes streams with _activeStreams.TryRemove directly (Lifecycle.cs:571), bypassing OnActiveStreamRemoved, so TryCompleteDrain never runs for a draining connection. Manager side: a dead connection still in _connections is disposed only when a later SelectConnection for the same key evicts it (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:196-199, 510-513); a connection already moved to _draining after GOAWAY is not disposed by EvictIfUnusable (TryRemoveExact returns false, Http2ConnectionManager.cs:507-508) and is later pruned from _draining without Dispose (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:517-521).

**Failure scenario.** (a) Server closes an idle HTTP/2 connection with FIN/RST and no GOAWAY, or the client detects a protocol error with no request in flight: the client keeps its socket and TLS state open (never sends FIN) until the next request to that origin or transport disposal - one lingering half-open socket per origin key. (b) Server sends GOAWAY during a deploy while a long request is in flight, the manager retires the connection to _draining, then the server drops TCP: the streams fail, but the socket/TLS stream is never disposed and the connection is dropped from _draining unreferenced; the descriptor is released only by finalization. RFC 9113 5.4.1 requires closing the TCP connection after the GOAWAY of a connection error.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 5.4.1

## Suggested fix
Make every terminal failure path own the close: after FailAllStreams in the read-loop catch blocks and in FailConnectionAfterWriteError, schedule Dispose() (thread pool, as TryCompleteDrain does), or have FailAllStreams itself do so; do not prune _draining entries without disposing them.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every terminal failure path (read-loop exception, frame write failure, protocol error) closes the connection by scheduling Dispose off the read loop
- [ ] A server FIN/RST with no request in flight results in the client closing its socket without waiting for the next request
- [ ] _draining entries are never pruned without being disposed
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-protocol-02` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: protocol-impl.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. The read-loop catch blocks (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:90-120) and FailConnectionAfterWriteError (Send.cs:94-107) only call FailAllStreams, which cancels _cts and fails streams (Lifecycle.cs:549-581) and never calls Dispose/DisposeStreamOnce; Dispose is reached only from Liveness.cs:224, Lifecycle.cs:509 (send stall) and TryCompleteDrain (Admission.cs:211-214). FailAllStreams removes streams with _activeStreams.TryRemove directly (Lifecycle.cs:571), not through OnActiveStreamRemoved, so a draining connection never reaches TryCompleteDrain. Manager: a dead connection still published is disposed only when a later SelectConnection for the same key hits it (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:196-199 -> 510-513) or via EvictIfUnusable after a failed in-flight dispatch (RawSocketTransport.cs:277-281), so an idle connection that gets EOF/RST without GOAWAY keeps its socket and TLS stream open until the next request to that origin or transport disposal. For a connection already retired to _draining, EvictIfUnusable -> RemoveExactAndRetire returns at TryRemoveExact==false (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:507-508) and the prune loop at 517-521 drops !IsAlive entries without disposing them: socket, CTS and the HPACK encoder buffer are left to finalization. Mitigation found: with a request in flight on a non-draining connection the dispatch failure path does dispose it, and a graceful GOAWAY with no streams closes inline (ReadLoop.cs HandleGoAwayFrame -> TryCompleteDrain(inline:true)). RFC 9113 5.4.1 (close TCP after the GOAWAY of a connection error) is not met on the idle path.

Also reported as `http2-runtime-11` (merged into this issue).

Related: [[R11-http2-runtime-24]], [[R11-http2-design-25]].

title: [HTTP/2] HandleDataFrameAsync repeats the same abort sequence five times and frames are written through four different paths
body:
## Summary
HandleDataFrameAsync contains five hand-copied blocks that debit the connection window, send a connection WINDOW_UPDATE, remove the stream, fault the body, track the reset and send RST_STREAM. Frames are written through four separate paths with different failure policies, and some helpers use closures despite the no-closures-per-frame rule. A rule added to one block is easily missed in the others.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:171`

## Problem
HandleDataFrameAsync (ReadLoop.cs:171-358) contains five hand-copied blocks of 'debit connection window, MaybeSendConnectionWindowUpdateAsync, RemoveActiveStream, Fail/FaultResponseBody, TrackRecentlyResetStream, SendRstStreamAsync' (lines 220-232, 236-248, 258-271, 275-283, 309-320) that already differ in detail (two skip the stream-window debit, two use Fail and two FaultResponseBody, one delegates to ResetMalformedResponseAsync). Outbound frames are produced four ways: WriteFrameLockedAsync (Send.cs:75-92, fails the connection on error), raw _codec.WriteFrameAsync(new Http2Frame{...}) under _writeLock for SETTINGS/PING ACKs and the initial SETTINGS (Http2Connection.cs:236-243, ReadLoop.cs:899-909, 944-954, allocating a frame object each), SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync with a per-call closure and a pooled 4/8-byte rental (Lifecycle.cs:34-128), and a hand-assembled frame header in SendGoAwayOnDisposeBestEffort (Lifecycle.cs:670-717), which duplicates both the codec's header serialisation and SendGoAwayAsync's payload (Lifecycle.cs:50-70).

**Failure scenario.** A rule added to one abort block (for example the stream-window debit, or tracking the reset) is missed in the others; a write-failure policy change in WriteFrameLockedAsync does not apply to the ACK writers. The closures in the WINDOW_UPDATE/RST_STREAM helpers also contradict the 'no closures per frame' rule of CLAUDE.md section 4.

## Suggested fix
One 'reject DATA and reset stream' helper parameterised by error and fault kind; one frame-writing primitive that takes a small stack/struct payload (two ints cover every control frame here) and applies the same failure policy everywhere, including the dispose-time GOAWAY.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The reject-DATA-and-reset sequence is one helper parameterised by error and fault kind
- [ ] One frame-writing primitive with a struct payload applies the same failure policy to control frames, ACKs and the dispose-time GOAWAY
- [ ] No closure is allocated per WINDOW_UPDATE or RST_STREAM frame
- [ ] Existing HTTP/2 DATA rejection tests keep passing unchanged
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context

title: [HTTP/2] HEADERS and DATA on a stream already closed by END_STREAM are tolerated instead of raising connection error STREAM_CLOSED
body:
## Summary
When DATA arrives for a stream not in _activeStreams, the client counts it against the connection window and answers RST_STREAM(STREAM_CLOSED) unless the id was recently reset. HEADERS for an inactive stream are decoded and ignored. RFC 9113 section 5.1 requires a connection error STREAM_CLOSED for frames received on a stream closed by END_STREAM. A hostile server can make the client do wasted work per frame indefinitely.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:203`

## Problem
HandleDataFrameAsync: when the stream is not in _activeStreams the frame is counted against the connection window and answered with RST_STREAM(STREAM_CLOSED) unless the id is in _recentlyResetStreams (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:203-212). CompleteHeaderBlock: a field block for an inactive stream is decoded and dropped silently (ReadLoop.cs:532-536). No state distinguishes 'closed by our RST_STREAM' (frames must be tolerated) from 'closed after the peer's END_STREAM'. RFC 9113 5.1 (closed): 'an endpoint that receives any frames after receiving a frame with the END_STREAM flag set MUST treat that as a connection error of type STREAM_CLOSED' (WINDOW_UPDATE/RST_STREAM/PRIORITY excepted). The test ClosedStream_FramesOnCompletedId_AreTolerated (Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2ConnectionTests.IdleStreamAndPreface.cs:93-125) asserts the leniency for DATA.

**Failure scenario.** A buggy or hostile server keeps sending HEADERS/DATA on stream ids whose exchange completed normally: the client decodes every block, replenishes the connection window and writes one RST_STREAM per DATA frame indefinitely, where the RFC requires GOAWAY(STREAM_CLOSED). Impact is limited to wasted work (1:1, no amplification).

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 5.1

## Suggested fix
Keep a bounded record of ids closed by a received END_STREAM (or the highest fully-closed id plus the recently-reset set) and raise the connection error for DATA/HEADERS on them; or document the leniency as deliberate in the code and the test.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] DATA or HEADERS on a stream id closed by a received END_STREAM raises a connection error STREAM_CLOSED (GOAWAY), using a bounded record of closed ids
- [ ] Frames on recently reset streams keep the tolerated behaviour required by RFC 9113 section 5.1
- [ ] The record of closed ids is bounded in size
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context

title: [HTTP/2] Response field blocks with a pseudo-header after a regular field or a repeated :status are accepted
body:
## Summary
ApplyDecodedHeaders does not track whether a regular field was already added, so a pseudo-header after a regular field is accepted, and a second :status silently overwrites the first, so the last one wins. RFC 9113 section 8.3 requires such responses to be treated as malformed with a stream error PROTOCOL_ERROR. An intermediary that disagrees with the client about which :status applies can be used for response confusion.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:626`

## Problem
ApplyDecodedHeaders loops over the decoded list (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:626-669): the `name == ":status"` branch does not check whether a regular field was already added to responseHeaders, and sets hasStatus/statusCode again on every occurrence, so the last :status wins. HpackDecoder.Decode performs no such check either. :status is parsed with int.TryParse(NumberStyles.None) and a 100..999 range (ReadLoop.cs:636-637), so `0200` or `00404` are also accepted although the status code is exactly three digits. rg over Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2 finds no test for pseudo-header ordering or duplicates.

**Failure scenario.** Server (or a compromised/buggy intermediary) sends HEADERS `content-type: x`, `:status: 200`, or `:status: 200` followed by `:status: 500`: RFC 9113 8.3 requires a stream error PROTOCOL_ERROR (malformed response); the client instead delivers a response, using the last :status. An intermediary that validated or logged the first :status and this client disagree on the response status.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Sections 8.3, 8.3.2, 8.1.1

## Suggested fix
Track `sawRegularField` and `hasStatus` in the loop: reject (RejectMalformedResponse) a pseudo-header that follows a regular field and a second :status; require the :status value to be exactly three ASCII digits.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A pseudo-header after a regular field in a response block is rejected through RejectMalformedResponse (PROTOCOL_ERROR)
- [ ] A second :status in one block is rejected as malformed
- [ ] A :status value that is not exactly three ASCII digits is rejected
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-protocol-04` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: rfc-compat.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: ApplyDecodedHeaders (ReadLoop.cs:624-669): the ':status' branch (626-644) neither checks that responseHeaders is still empty nor that hasStatus is already set, so a pseudo-header after a regular field and a repeated :status are accepted with the last value winning; HpackDecoder documents that it returns pseudo-headers mixed (HpackDecoder.cs:43) and does no ordering check. int.TryParse(NumberStyles.None) with 100..999 (636-637) accepts '0200'. RFC 9113 8.3 requires both cases to be treated as malformed (stream error). rg over Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2 finds only the unknown-pseudo-header test (Http2ConnectionTests.ProtocolAndCleanup.cs:441), nothing for ordering or duplicates. No interop impact with conformant servers; strictness/RFC MUST gap.

title: [HTTP/2] Malformed-response error messages echo unvalidated peer-controlled :status values and pseudo-header names
body:
## Summary
RejectMalformedResponse builds messages with the raw :status value and unknown pseudo-header name received from the peer. These strings pass no character or length validation, so they can hold CR/LF and up to the header-list limit of bytes. The resulting UHttpException message reaches monitors, recordings and log sinks verbatim, enabling log forgery.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:643`

## Problem
RejectMalformedResponse(stream, $"Invalid :status value: {value}") (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:643) and $"Unexpected pseudo-header in trailing headers: {name}" / "...in response headers: {name}" (ReadLoop.cs:661, 666) interpolate strings that have passed no character or length validation (the pseudo-header branches run before/without GetMalformedResponseFieldReason); the text becomes UHttpError.Message of the exception delivered to handlers and logs. GetMalformedResponseFieldReason documents the opposite intent ('a reason that never echoes the value', ReadLoop.cs:754-755).

**Failure scenario.** A hostile server sends `:status: 200\r\n[ERROR] forged log line ...` or a 60 KB pseudo-header name: the request fails with a UHttpException whose message contains up to the header-list limit of attacker-chosen bytes including CR/LF, which monitors, recordings and log sinks print verbatim (log forging / log bloat).

## Suggested fix
Do not echo the value or an unvalidated name: report 'invalid :status' and 'unexpected pseudo-header', or include at most a short, sanitized (printable ASCII, truncated) name.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Messages report 'invalid :status' and 'unexpected pseudo-header' without the peer value, or include at most a short truncated name restricted to printable ASCII
- [ ] An exception message for a hostile :status or pseudo-header name contains no CR, LF or other control characters and is bounded in length
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context

title: [HTTP/2] Response trailers skip the prohibited-trailer filter that HTTP/1.1 applies
body:
## Summary
The HTTP/1.1 parser drops trailer fields listed in TrailerFieldValidator.IsProhibitedResponseTrailer, such as cache-control, content-encoding, location and www-authenticate. The HTTP/2 trailer branch of ApplyDecodedHeaders does not apply the filter. The same response therefore exposes those fields through GetTrailersAsync over HTTP/2 to cache, decompression and application code, while HTTP/1.1 hides them (RFC 9110 section 6.5.1).

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:694`

## Problem
HTTP/1.1 drops prohibited response trailers: Http11ResponseParser.AddResponseTrailer returns false for TrailerFieldValidator.IsProhibitedResponseTrailer (Http11ResponseParser.cs:740-758; the list in Runtime/Transport/Internal/TrailerFieldValidator.cs:8-45 covers Content-Length, Transfer-Encoding, Content-Encoding, Content-Type, Authorization, WWW-Authenticate, Cache-Control, Location, Vary, ...). HTTP/2 passes the decoded trailer block straight through: ApplyDecodedHeaders only runs GetMalformedResponseFieldReason and then stream.AppendTrailers(responseHeaders) (ReadLoop.cs:647-658, 694). The only use of the validator in Http2/ is for request trailers (Http2Connection.Send.cs:432).

**Failure scenario.** A server (or intermediary) that puts cache-control, content-encoding, location or www-authenticate into a trailer section: over HTTP/1.1 the fields are dropped, over HTTP/2 the same response exposes them through GetTrailersAsync to cache, decompression and application code. Behaviour depends on the negotiated protocol, and fields RFC 9110 Section 6.5.1 says must not be honoured from trailers reach consumers on one path only.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 Section 6.5.1

## Suggested fix
Apply TrailerFieldValidator.IsProhibitedResponseTrailer in the trailer branch of ApplyDecodedHeaders (skip the field, as HTTP/1.1 does) and add a test mirroring the HTTP/1.1 one.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The HTTP/2 trailer branch skips fields for which TrailerFieldValidator.IsProhibitedResponseTrailer is true
- [ ] HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 expose the same trailer set for the same prohibited fields
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-design-10` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: code-smell.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Code is as described: HTTP/1.1 drops prohibited response trailers (Http11ResponseParser.cs:741-758, TrailerFieldValidator.cs:8-55), while the HTTP/2 trailer branch only runs GetMalformedResponseFieldReason and calls stream.AppendTrailers(responseHeaders) (ReadLoop.cs:647-658, 694); the only validator use in Http2/ is for request trailers (Send.cs:432). Severity lowered: trailers are kept in a separate collection end to end (Http2Stream.cs:452-455 -> GetTrailersAsync -> UHttpResponse.Trailers; the cache stores them as trailers, CacheInterceptor.cs:566, 761, 794) and nothing merges them into the header section, so RFC 9110 Section 6.5.1 is not violated and cache/decompression do not act on them. What remains is a protocol-dependent difference in what the application sees in Trailers.

Also reported as `http2-protocol-18` (merged into this issue).

title: [HTTP/2] Interim 1xx responses are bounded on HTTP/1.1 by Max1xxResponses but unbounded on HTTP/2
body:
## Summary
HTTP/1.1 counts interim responses and fails with 'Too many 1xx interim responses'. The HTTP/2 path accepts any number of 1xx HEADERS on a stream, keeping the stream and its concurrency slot open and the read loop decoding until the request timeout. A streamed response already handed off has no request deadline at all.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:703`

## Problem
HTTP/1.1 counts interim responses and fails with 'Too many 1xx interim responses' (Http11ResponseParser.cs:251-253; RawSocketTransport.cs:2275-2282). The HTTP/2 path accepts any number of 1xx HEADERS on a stream: ApplyDecodedHeaders returns after an optional SignalExpectContinueContinue with no counter (ReadLoop.cs:703-717), and HeadersReceived stays false so the next block is treated as a first response again.

**Failure scenario.** A peer that streams 1xx field blocks keeps the stream (and its concurrency slot) open and the read loop busy decoding them until the request timeout; on HTTP/1.1 the same behaviour is cut off after Max1xxResponses. A streamed response that was already handed off has no request deadline at all.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 8.1

## Suggested fix
Count interim responses per stream and fail the stream (PROTOCOL_ERROR / ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM) above the same Max1xxResponses constant.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Interim responses are counted per stream and the stream is failed with PROTOCOL_ERROR or ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM above the same Max1xxResponses constant used by HTTP/1.1
- [ ] The failure surfaces to the caller as a UHttpException
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context

title: [HTTP/2] Response field-name validation is duplicated in three copies and the HTTP/2 copy accepts non-token names
body:
## Summary
Requests use HttpFieldValidator and HTTP/1.1 responses use an RFC 9110 token check, but HTTP/2 responses use a hand-written check in GetMalformedResponseFieldReason that only rejects empty names, upper-case letters and bytes outside 0x21-0x7E. Delimiters such as ':' ',' ';' '=' pass. The two connection-specific header lists (IsConnectionSpecificField and IsHttp2ForbiddenHeader) are also separate copies. A name accepted on HTTP/2 is rejected on HTTP/1.1.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:757`

## Problem
Requests share HttpFieldValidator (RFC 9110 token names, Runtime/Transport/Internal/HttpFieldValidator.cs:53-76). HTTP/1.1 responses use IsValidHeaderFieldName = EncodingHelper.IsRfc9110TChar for every character (Http11ResponseParser.cs:955-968). HTTP/2 responses use a third, hand-written check, GetMalformedResponseFieldReason (ReadLoop.cs:757-790): it only rejects empty names, 'A'-'Z' and characters <= 0x20 or >= 0x7F, so delimiters such as ':' '(' ',' ';' '"' '=' '@' pass. RFC 9113 Section 8.2.1 additionally forbids a colon in a non-pseudo field name. Likewise IsConnectionSpecificField (ReadLoop.cs:792-805) and IsHttp2ForbiddenHeader (Send.cs:560-568) are two separate lists of the connection-specific fields.

**Failure scenario.** An HTTP/2 response with a field named 'x:y' or 'a,b' is accepted and stored in HttpHeaders, while the same name is rejected on HTTP/1.1. Code that re-serialises headers as 'name: value' lines (cache storage, record/replay, logging) then produces a line that parses back as a different field.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 8.2.1

## Suggested fix
Use one response-field validator for both protocols (tchar names, lower-case requirement added for HTTP/2) and one shared list of connection-specific fields.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] HTTP/2 response field names are validated with the same RFC 9110 tchar rule as HTTP/1.1, plus the lower-case requirement of RFC 9113 Section 8.2.1
- [ ] One shared list of connection-specific fields is used by the HTTP/2 send and receive paths
- [ ] A response with a non-token field name such as 'a,b' is treated as malformed on HTTP/2
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context

title: [HTTP/2] Response field names containing ':' after the first character are accepted instead of making the response malformed
body:
## Summary
GetMalformedResponseFieldReason has no check for 0x3A, and only names that start with ':' are routed to the pseudo-header branch. A response field such as 'x:y' is stored in HttpHeaders. RFC 9113 Section 8.2.1 forbids a colon in a field name and requires the message to be treated as malformed. Consumers that re-serialise headers in HTTP/1.1 form (cache, recording, relays) can turn such a field into a different field.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:762`

## Problem
GetMalformedResponseFieldReason (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:757-790) rejects A-Z, c <= 0x20 and c >= 0x7F in names but has no check for 0x3A; ApplyDecodedHeaders only routes names that START with ':' to the pseudo-header branch (ReadLoop.cs:647). A name such as `x:y` is added to HttpHeaders (HttpHeaders.Add validates only null/whitespace, Runtime/Core/HttpHeaders.cs:49-54).

**Failure scenario.** A response carries the field name `set-cookie:x` or `foo:bar`. RFC 9113 8.2.1 says a field name MUST NOT contain a colon and the message MUST be treated as malformed; the client surfaces it. Any consumer that serializes headers in HTTP/1.1 form (recording, cache store, a relay) turns `foo:bar: v` into field `foo` with value `bar: v` - a header-injection primitive for whoever controls the upstream field name.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 8.2.1

## Suggested fix
Reject ':' at any index of a regular field name in GetMalformedResponseFieldReason (the pseudo-header branch already handles a leading ':').

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A regular response field name containing ':' at any index makes the response malformed (stream error PROTOCOL_ERROR)
- [ ] The leading ':' pseudo-header branch behaves as before
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it
