title: [HTTP/2] Unparsable, overflowing or conflicting response content-length values are ignored instead of making the response malformed
body:
## Summary
GetContentLength reads only the first content-length value and treats a parse failure or overflow as 'no content-length', so the DATA-length checks are skipped. Repeated or conflicting values are never compared and remain in the headers handed to handlers. RFC 9110 Section 8.6 and RFC 9113 Section 8.1.1 make such a response malformed.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:807`

## Problem
GetContentLength (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:807-819) reads only the first value (HttpHeaders.Get) and returns null when long.TryParse fails or the value overflows; null means 'no content-length', so ExpectedResponseBodyLength stays -1 (Http2Stream.cs:269-271) and the DATA-sum checks at ReadLoop.cs:273-283 and 334-340 are skipped. A second, different content-length field line is never looked at; the header list handed to the handler still contains the invalid or conflicting values.

**Failure scenario.** Response with `content-length: 10` and `content-length: 20`, or `content-length: 5, 7`, or `content-length: abc`, or a 20-digit value: RFC 9110 8.6 makes these invalid and RFC 9113 8.1.1 makes the response malformed (stream error PROTOCOL_ERROR). The client accepts the response, validates against the first value only (or against nothing), and hands the bogus field to caches/handlers that may trust it.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 Section 8.6; RFC 9113 Section 8.1.1

## Suggested fix
Validate all content-length field lines: every value must be 1*DIGIT within long range and all values equal; otherwise RejectMalformedResponse.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every content-length field line and every comma-separated value must be 1*DIGIT within long range and all values equal; otherwise the response is rejected as malformed (PROTOCOL_ERROR stream error)
- [ ] A valid single content-length keeps the existing DATA-sum checks
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] New peer SETTINGS values are used by concurrent senders before the SETTINGS ACK is written
body:
## Summary
HandleSettingsFrameAsync applies the new values and wakes blocked senders, and only then waits for the write lock to send the ACK. A sender already queued on the write lock can emit frames sized with the new MAX_FRAME_SIZE, window or HPACK table size before the ACK. A peer that activates its settings on ACK (for example nghttp2) still enforces the old limits and can answer with a connection error. Unconfirmed against a real peer.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:846`

## Problem
HandleSettingsFrameAsync applies the values under _streamCreateLock (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:846-891), wakes blocked senders (893-894) and only then queues for _writeLock to write the ACK (899-909). A sender already holding or queued on _writeLock reads the new _remoteSettings.MaxFrameSize / stream window / pending HPACK size update (Http2Connection.Send.cs:25, 199-203; HpackEncoder.cs:63-64) and writes HEADERS/DATA built with them ahead of the ACK. RFC 9113 6.5.3: the recipient 'MUST immediately emit a SETTINGS frame with the ACK flag set' once the values are processed, and the sender may rely on them only after the ACK. Receivers that activate their own settings on ACK (nghttp2: local_settings updated in session_update_local_settings when the ACK arrives) still enforce the old MAX_FRAME_SIZE / window / header table limit at that point. The initial server SETTINGS is safe (no dispatch before InitializeAsync returns).

**Failure scenario.** A server raises SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE (or INITIAL_WINDOW_SIZE, or HEADER_TABLE_SIZE) mid-connection while an upload is in progress: the uploader that holds _writeLock next sends a 32 KiB DATA frame (or a table size update above the old limit) before the ACK; an nghttp2-style peer answers FRAME_SIZE_ERROR / FLOW_CONTROL_ERROR / COMPRESSION_ERROR and the connection dies. Needs a peer that changes settings upward mid-connection and enforces them at ACK time (confirm with an nghttp2-based server in Tools~/h2-interop).

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 6.5.3; RFC 7541 Section 4.2

## Suggested fix
Write the ACK in the same _writeLock hold in which increases become visible: take _writeLock first, apply the settings (still under _streamCreateLock for the window delta), write the ACK, release; decreases may be applied immediately.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Increases from a peer SETTINGS frame become visible to senders only in the same write-lock hold that writes the ACK
- [ ] A test with a sender queued on the write lock shows no frame using the new value is written before the ACK
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] HPACK encoder dynamic table grows to the server's SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE (up to 2^31-1) with a linear scan per header
body:
## Summary
The encoder table size is set to whatever SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE the peer sends, clamped only to int.MaxValue. Every non-sensitive field is added to a LinkedList that FindMatch scans linearly. A hostile or misconfigured server can make memory grow without bound on a long-lived connection and make encoding under the write lock slower with every request. This breaks the rule that every peer-controlled size is bounded.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:857`

## Problem
Http2Settings.Apply stores the peer value clamped only to int.MaxValue (Http2Settings.cs:49-51); HandleSettingsFrameAsync passes it straight to _hpackEncoder.SetMaxDynamicTableSize (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:857-858); ApplyPendingSizeUpdates sets the table max to it and announces it (HpackEncoder.cs:131-156). Encode adds every non-sensitive field to the table with incremental indexing, including unique values such as :path with a query, content-length, custom ids (HpackEncoder.cs:74-93). HpackDynamicTable is a LinkedList scanned linearly by FindMatch for every header (HpackDynamicTable.cs:90-121). RFC 7541 4.2 lets the encoder choose any size up to the peer's limit; nothing caps it locally. Http2SettingsTests (line 50-54) only assert the clamp to int.MaxValue.

**Failure scenario.** A hostile or misconfigured server sends SETTINGS_HEADER_TABLE_SIZE=0x7fffffff. On a long-lived connection each request with a unique :path/header value adds entries that are never evicted: memory grows without bound (two .NET strings plus a list node per entry), and every header of every later request walks the whole list (100k requests -> ~100k string comparisons per header, per request), so request encoding - done under _writeLock - degrades until the connection is unusable. Violates the 'every peer-controlled size is bounded' rule.

## Spec reference
RFC 7541 Sections 4.2 and 7.3; RFC 9113 Section 10.5

## Suggested fix
Cap the encoder table at a local limit (4096, or a small option) with Math.Min(peerValue, cap) before SetMaxDynamicTableSize; the size update then announces the capped value, which RFC 7541 4.2 permits.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The encoder table size is Math.Min(peer value, a local cap) (4096 by default) and the announced size update carries the capped value
- [ ] Memory held by the encoder table stays within the cap for a peer advertising 0x7fffffff
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-protocol-03` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: security.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Code is as described and no cap exists anywhere: Http2Settings.cs:49-51 stores ClampToIntMax(value); ReadLoop.cs:857-858 passes it to HpackEncoder.SetMaxDynamicTableSize; ApplyPendingSizeUpdates (HpackEncoder.cs:131-156) sets the table max to it; the only construction is `new HpackEncoder()` (Http2Connection.cs:176) and rg finds no Math.Min on HeaderTableSize. Encode adds every non-sensitive NameMatch/None field (HpackEncoder.cs:78-90) and HpackDynamicTable.FindMatch walks the whole LinkedList for every field that is not a static full match (HpackDynamicTable.cs:90-121). So with a peer-sent 2^31-1 the table grows by one entry per unique :path/header value for the life of the connection and each later header costs O(entries) under _writeLock. Growth is paced by the client's own requests, so it is slow-burn rather than an instant DoS, but it is an unbounded peer-controlled size (CLAUDE.md section 3) and the per-header linear scan is already measurable at legitimate values such as 65536. HpackEncoderTableSizeTests only cover size-update signalling.

Also reported as `http2-runtime-15` (merged into this issue).

Related: #406.

title: [HTTP/2] A PRIORITY frame with a wrong length or a self-dependency fails the whole connection instead of one stream
body:
## Summary
HandlePriorityFrame throws a connection error for a length other than 5 and for a stream that depends on itself. RFC 9113 Section 6.3 makes a wrong length a stream error of type FRAME_SIZE_ERROR, and RFC 9113 dropped the self-dependency rule together with the priority scheme. One bad PRIORITY frame therefore fails every in-flight request on the connection. The existing test asserts the non-conformant GOAWAY.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:1117`

## Problem
HandlePriorityFrame throws Http2ProtocolException(FrameSizeError) for Length != 5 and Http2ProtocolException(ProtocolError) when the dependency equals the stream id (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:1110-1126); both are caught by the read loop as connection errors (GOAWAY + FailAllStreams, ReadLoop.cs:107-116). RFC 9113 6.3: 'A PRIORITY frame with a length other than 5 octets MUST be treated as a stream error of type FRAME_SIZE_ERROR'; RFC 7540 5.3.1 made self-dependency a stream error and RFC 9113 dropped the rule with the priority scheme. The test Priority_InvalidLength_SendsFrameSizeErrorGoAway (Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2ConnectionTests.FrameHandling.cs:340-370) asserts the GOAWAY, i.e. the non-conformant behaviour.

**Failure scenario.** A server sends a 4-byte PRIORITY frame, or a PRIORITY whose dependency is its own stream, for stream 5 while 30 other requests are in flight: all 30 fail with a connection error (idempotent ones are replayed once) instead of only stream 5 being reset.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Sections 6.3, 4.2, 5.3.2

## Suggested fix
For a non-zero stream id send RST_STREAM(FRAME_SIZE_ERROR) (failing that stream if active) for a bad length and ignore the dependency field entirely; update the test.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A PRIORITY frame with length other than 5 on a non-zero stream results in RST_STREAM(FRAME_SIZE_ERROR) for that stream only
- [ ] The dependency field is ignored, so a self-dependency is not an error
- [ ] Other streams on the connection continue
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it; Priority_InvalidLength_SendsFrameSizeErrorGoAway is updated

title: [HTTP/2] No per-client or per-request switch to disable h2, and HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED is handled as a generic stream error
body:
## Summary
Direct TLS connections always offer h2 and http/1.1 in ALPN, and Http2Options has no enable switch. HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED exists only in the error-code enum, so a server that answers RST_STREAM(HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED) makes the request fail and every retry reuses the same h2 connection. On Unity h2 is reached only with the opt-in BouncyCastle backend, and a client-level workaround exists through TlsBackend, so this is a missing capability rather than a protocol violation.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:1152`

## Problem
Direct TLS connections always offer AlpnProtocols.H2AndHttp11 (Runtime/Transport/Tcp/TcpConnectionPool.cs:685); Http2Options has no enable/version switch (only EnableHttp2ThroughConnectTunnels, whose doc at Http2Options.cs:163-171 states direct connections always offer h2). Once an origin has an h2 connection every request takes the fast path (RawSocketTransport.cs:584-593). Http2ErrorCode.Http11Required (0xd) exists only in the enum (Http2Frame.cs:55): HandleRstStreamFrame special-cases REFUSED_STREAM alone and maps everything else to NetworkError 'RST_STREAM: Http11Required' (ReadLoop.cs:1141-1155); GOAWAY is handled the same way (ReadLoop.cs:1019-1026).

**Failure scenario.** An endpoint that answers RST_STREAM(HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED) (servers do this for resources that need connection-level auth or a TLS client certificate) fails every time: retries go back to the same h2 connection, and the application cannot force HTTP/1.1 for that client or request. The same missing switch means a client that suffers the known 3x HTTP/2 streaming slowdown (#406) or a broken h2 middlebox cannot fall back short of removing the TLS provider that supplies ALPN.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 7 (HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED), Section 8.7

## Suggested fix
Add a protocol policy (per client, ideally per request) that controls the ALPN offer and the h2 fast path, and handle HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED by replaying the unprocessed request on an HTTP/1.1-only connection and remembering that for the origin.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A protocol policy (per client, and per request if feasible) controls the ALPN offer and use of the h2 fast path
- [ ] RST_STREAM and GOAWAY with HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED cause the unprocessed request to be replayed on an HTTP/1.1 connection and the origin is remembered as HTTP/1.1-only
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it
- [ ] public API additions have XML docs

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-design-19` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: architecture.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Code is as described, but the 'no way to opt out' half is overstated. Confirmed: direct TLS dials always offer AlpnProtocols.H2AndHttp11 (TcpConnectionPool.cs:685); Http2Options has no enable switch (only EnableHttp2ThroughConnectTunnels, Http2Options.cs:163-175); Http2ErrorCode.Http11Required appears only in the enum (Http2Frame.cs:55, rg finds no other use); HandleRstStreamFrame marks only REFUSED_STREAM retryable and turns every other code into NetworkError 'RST_STREAM: <code>' (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:1141-1155); the transport replay loop acts only on Http2RetryableRequestException (RawSocketTransport.cs:531-548), so an HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED reset fails the request and any later retry reuses the same h2 connection (584-593). Mitigations the finding underplays: (1) on Unity h2 is reached only with the explicit opt-in TlsBackend.BouncyCastle; the default Auto and SslStream never negotiate ALPN and stay on HTTP/1.1 (TlsBackend.cs:18-30, SslStreamTlsProvider.cs:20-26, #418), and TlsBackend is a per-client option (UHttpClientOptions.cs:171), so a client-level HTTP/1.1-only route exists (a second client on SslStream), though it couples protocol choice to the TLS stack and gives no per-request or per-origin control; (2) RFC 9113 Section 7 only defines HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED and no section requires a client to replay on HTTP/1.1, so this is a missing feature, not a protocol violation. Becomes more important once a native ALPN backend lands (#429). No open issue tracks a protocol policy or HTTP_1_1_REQUIRED fallback (#121 API review does not list it). Downgraded to low: feature gap reachable only under an opt-in backend, with a coarse workaround.

Related: #121, #406, #429.

title: [HTTP/2] SendBufferedDataAsync awaits _writeLock without ConfigureAwait(false) and can resume on the Unity main thread
body:
## Summary
The await on _writeLock at Send.cs:189 is the only dispatch-path await without ConfigureAwait(false). An upload started from the main thread on a warm connection can resume on UnitySynchronizationContext while holding the connection write lock, blocking all other writes until the main thread runs. platform.md requires library code not to rely on the caller's SynchronizationContext. Plausible, not reproduced.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Send.cs:189`

## Problem
'await _writeLock.WaitAsync(ct);' (Send.cs:189) is the only await on the dispatch path without ConfigureAwait(false); the others without it are on Task.Run loops or after the dial (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:307, 333; Http2Connection.cs:232-243; Http2FrameCodec.cs:117, 136, 250-252, 260). Core does not leave the caller's context before the transport (RawSocketTransport.cs:141-175), and on the connection-reuse path AcquireStreamSlotAsync, the HEADERS lock wait and the HEADERS write can all complete synchronously, so the method can still run on the caller's SynchronizationContext when it reaches line 189. platform.md: library code never relies on the caller's SynchronizationContext (#245).

**Failure scenario.** A POST is sent from the main thread on a warm connection while another stream holds _writeLock; the lock is granted to a continuation posted to UnitySynchronizationContext. Until the next frame (or for as long as the main thread is blocked or paused) the connection's write lock is held and no other stream, WINDOW_UPDATE or PING ACK can be written. Whether the earlier writes complete synchronously depends on the socket I/O mode and runtime.

## Suggested fix
Add ConfigureAwait(false) at Send.cs:189 and to the remaining awaits listed above, and enable an analyzer (CA2007) for the Transport assembly so it cannot regress.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every await in Runtime/Transport/Http2 on the dispatch path uses ConfigureAwait(false)
- [ ] Analyzer CA2007 is enabled for the Transport assembly and the shadow build passes
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it (a custom SynchronizationContext asserts no continuation is posted to it)

title: [HTTP/2] Zero-length known-length streaming request body with a trailer provider sends no trailers or END_STREAM and the stream is cancelled
body:
## Summary
HasRequestBody returns true whenever a TrailerProvider is set, so HEADERS go out without END_STREAM and SendStreamingDataAsync runs. With ContentLength == 0 the known-length loop never executes and the method returns without trailers or an END_STREAM frame. DispatchAsync then sends RST_STREAM(CANCEL). A POST with an empty stream body and trailers is never completed.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Send.cs:262`

## Problem
ExpectContinueHelper.HasRequestBody returns true whenever TrailerProvider != null (Runtime/Transport/Internal/ExpectContinueHelper.cs:20-21), so DispatchAsync sends HEADERS without END_STREAM and calls SendDataAsync (Http2Connection.cs:414, 445). For a non-buffered body SendStreamingDataAsync takes the known-length branch: with session.ContentLength == 0 the `while (remaining.Value > 0)` loop never runs and the method returns at line 306 without collecting trailers or writing any frame (Http2Connection.Send.cs:262-307). Back in DispatchAsync stream.IsLocalClosed is false, so ResetStreamIfActiveAsync sends RST_STREAM(CANCEL) (Http2Connection.cs:448-455). The buffered path handles the empty case correctly (Send.cs:120-134), and the unknown-length path sends trailers or an empty END_STREAM DATA frame (Send.cs:321-334).

**Failure scenario.** POST with a stream-backed body whose Length is 0 (empty file / empty MemoryStream) and request trailers (e.g. a checksum trailer): the server receives HEADERS then RST_STREAM(CANCEL); the request is never completed and the dispatch waits for a response until the request timeout, or reports whatever the server did before the reset.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 8.1

## Suggested fix
After the known-length loop (and when it never ran) collect the trailers and send them, or send an empty END_STREAM DATA frame, exactly as the unknown-length branch does at EOF.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A known-length streaming body of length 0 with a trailer provider ends the stream by sending the trailers (or an empty END_STREAM DATA frame if there are none)
- [ ] No RST_STREAM(CANCEL) is sent for this request
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] An upload blocked on flow control after a complete response waits until the request deadline and then reports Timeout
body:
## Summary
WaitForSendWindowAsync returns only for a positive window or an aborted request body. Completing the response wakes the waiter but does not abort the body, so the uploader waits again. If the server answers early with a full response, stops reading and sends no RST_STREAM(NO_ERROR), the request stays open until its timeout and fails with Timeout although the response was delivered. Plausible; depends on the peer not resetting.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Send.cs:506`

## Problem
WaitForSendWindowAsync returns only when the window is positive or stream.IsRequestBodyAborted (Send.cs:506-510). Completion of the response wakes the waiters (Http2Stream.cs:771-778, whose comment says the uploader 'stops now') but does not set _requestBodyAborted, so the uploader re-checks and waits again; DispatchAsync is still inside SendDataAsync (Http2Connection.cs:445). The only exits are a peer WINDOW_UPDATE or RST_STREAM, or the request token, after which the transport maps the cancellation to Timeout and calls OnResponseError (RawSocketTransport.cs:178-181). The test StreamLifecycle_CompleteEarlyResponse_UploadContinuesUntilBodyEnds covers a peer that keeps granting window, FlowControl_EarlyFinalResponseAndRstNoError covers a peer that resets.

**Failure scenario.** A server answers a large upload early with a complete 4xx response, stops reading the body and does not send RST_STREAM(NO_ERROR) (it MAY, RFC 9113 Section 8.1). The handler has the full response, but the request stays open until its timeout and then fails with Timeout. Depends on the peer not resetting.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 8.1

## Suggested fix
When the response is complete (remote closed and handler done) and the uploader is blocked on the window, abandon the request body (MarkLocalAbandoned, RST_STREAM NO_ERROR or CANCEL) and complete the dispatch successfully.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] When the response is complete and the uploader is blocked on the send window, the request body is abandoned (RST_STREAM NO_ERROR or CANCEL) and the dispatch completes successfully
- [ ] The stale comment in Http2Stream.TrySetResult matches the behaviour
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] A timeout during an upload after the response started calls OnResponseError after OnResponseStart
body:
## Summary
The upload continues after the response starts. If it is blocked on flow control when the request deadline fires, the cancellation leaves DispatchAsync, is mapped to Timeout and RawSocketTransport calls handler.OnResponseError although OnResponseStartAsync already ran. The handler contract allows OnResponseError only before the response starts. The body read already fails with Timeout, so the remaining effect is an extra error callback seen by logging, monitor and cache handlers.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Send.cs:519`

## Problem
The upload deliberately continues after the response starts or completes (Http2Connection.cs:443-445). SendBufferedDataAsync loops on WaitForSendWindowAsync, which returns only for a positive window or IsRequestBodyAborted and throws ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() when the request token fires (Http2Connection.Send.cs:170-187, 493-521). Http2Stream.TrySetResult wakes the waiters with the comment 'an uploader blocked on the send window stops now' (Http2Stream.cs:771-779), but IsRequestBodyAborted (Http2Stream.cs:117-127) does not look at response completion, so the uploader just waits again. When the deadline fires, the OperationCanceledException leaves DispatchAsync through the filter at Http2Connection.cs:481-483 (not caught), RawSocketTransport.MapDispatchAttemptFailure turns it into UHttpErrorType.Timeout (RawSocketTransport.cs:799-803) and RawSocketTransport.DispatchAsync calls handler.OnResponseError (RawSocketTransport.cs:178-182) although OnResponseStartAsync already ran for this exchange. architecture.md ('Handler callbacks'): OnResponseError is only valid before the response starts.

**Failure scenario.** A server answers early (401/413 or a 200 that does not need the body) with END_STREAM, stops granting stream window and does not send RST_STREAM(NO_ERROR); or simply a slow upload whose response headers arrived first reaches request.Timeout while blocked on the window. The application already received the response, the stream slot stays occupied until the deadline, and then the handler chain gets a second outcome (OnResponseError(Timeout)) for a response that was started/completed - a retry or metrics handler acting on it sees a failed request. Which servers leave the stream half-open without RST_STREAM needs confirming; the deadline-during-upload half is peer-independent.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 8.1

## Suggested fix
Once the response has started, end the upload without throwing: on request-token cancellation in the upload path call AbortRequestBody and return (the body source already carries the Timeout/cancellation), and decide explicitly whether a completed response (END_STREAM received and handler done) abandons the remaining upload with RST_STREAM(NO_ERROR/CANCEL), as the stale comment in TrySetResult describes.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After the response has started, request-token cancellation in the upload path ends the upload (AbortRequestBody) without throwing and OnResponseError is not called
- [ ] The behaviour for a completed early response is decided explicitly and documented in code
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-protocol-15` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: protocol-impl.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: The callback half holds: with the response started and the upload blocked, the request token makes WaitForSendWindowAsync throw (Send.cs:504/519, also _writeLock.WaitAsync(ct) at Send.cs:189), the filter at Http2Connection.cs:481-483 lets the OCE through, MapDispatchAttemptFailure maps it to Timeout (RawSocketTransport.cs:799-803) and DispatchAsync calls handler.OnResponseError (RawSocketTransport.cs:178-182) although OnResponseStartAsync already ran, against IHttpHandler.cs:31-35. Tests RequestTimeout_DuringUploadAfterResponseStart_* cover the scenario but only assert the body-read error. Downgraded because the harm is contained: Stream.Cancel already faults the body with Timeout (Http2Stream.cs:522-541), HandlerCallbackSafetyWrapper drops a terminal callback after a completed response start (HandlerCallbackSafetyWrapper.cs:70-73, 88), MetricsHandler guards with _completionRecorded, and RetryInterceptor does not retry once committed (RetryInterceptor.cs:81). Remaining effect: intermediate handlers (logging/monitor/cache) see an extra OnResponseError. The 'completed response does not stop the upload' half is deliberate (Http2Connection.cs:443-445, test StreamLifecycle_CompleteEarlyResponse_UploadContinuesUntilBodyEnds) and only hurts if a server sends a full response, stops granting window and sends no RST_STREAM(NO_ERROR): peer-dependent, not settled statically. The TrySetResult comment (Http2Stream.cs:776-777) is stale: IsRequestBodyAborted (117-127) ignores completion.

title: [HTTP/2] A caller-supplied Host header is honoured on HTTP/1.1 and silently dropped on HTTP/2
body:
## Summary
HTTP/1.1 writes the caller's Host header, while HTTP/2 always builds :authority from the URI and discards Host via IsHttp2ForbiddenHeader. A request that sets Host to reach a virtual host on an IP URL works on HTTP/1.1 and is routed differently once h2 is negotiated, without any error. No test covers this.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.Send.cs:567`

## Problem
HTTP/1.1 only generates Host when the request has none and otherwise writes the caller's value (Http11RequestSerializer.cs:310-318, 320-336). HTTP/2 always builds :authority from the URI (Http2Connection.cs:308, 376) and discards a caller Host header via IsHttp2ForbiddenHeader (Send.cs:567). No test covers a caller Host header over HTTP/2 (Http2ConnectionTests.Authority.cs only asserts that no 'host' field is sent).

**Failure scenario.** A request to https://10.0.0.5/ (or a staging hostname) with WithHeader('Host', 'api.example.com') reaches the intended virtual host on HTTP/1.1; when the same endpoint negotiates h2 the override disappears without an error and the request is routed by the URI authority instead.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 8.3.1

## Suggested fix
Decide once for both protocols: either map a valid caller Host to :authority on HTTP/2 (what RFC 9113 Section 8.3.1 expects from a client translating a request) or reject/ignore a caller Host on both, and test it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Host handling is the same on both protocols: a valid caller Host is mapped to :authority on HTTP/2, or it is rejected or ignored on both
- [ ] The chosen behaviour is documented in the XML docs of the header API
- [ ] a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/Http2/ fails before the fix and passes after it

title: [HTTP/2] Http2Connection is a 3,650-line class over six partial files split by file rather than responsibility
body:
## Summary
The partial files do not follow responsibilities: Lifecycle holds stream-id allocation, frame senders, flow control, liveness scans and Dispose, and read-loop state is declared outside the read-loop file. About 60 fields have four owners distinguished only by comments, and DispatchAsync is a 230-line method. architecture.md still lists only three of the six partial files. This is a maintainability finding, not a traced defect.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.cs:19`

## Problem
Http2Connection spans Http2Connection.cs (669), .ReadLoop.cs (1206), .Send.cs (570), .Lifecycle.cs (719), .Admission.cs (217), .Liveness.cs (269). Responsibilities do not follow the files: .Lifecycle.cs ('Helpers and lifecycle', line 12) holds stream-id allocation, WINDOW_UPDATE/GOAWAY/RST_STREAM senders, the active-stream map, request cancellation, recently-reset tracking, receive-side flow control (lines 353-446), the maintenance loop and stall scans, FailAllStreams and Dispose; send-side flow control is in .Send.cs; read-loop state such as _continuationStreamId/_headerBlock* is declared in Http2Connection.cs (lines 97-107) but owned by .ReadLoop.cs. One class has about 70 fields with four owners (read loop, _writeLock, _streamCreateLock, Interlocked) distinguished only by comments. DispatchAsync is a 230-line method tracking five booleans (Http2Connection.cs:295-527); ApplyDecodedHeaders mixes HTTP semantics (pseudo-headers, content-length, 1xx, trailers) with stream state transitions (ReadLoop.cs:604-751). architecture.md line 81 still lists only .ReadLoop, .Send, .Lifecycle. The inline issue references (#29, #181, #197, #318, #320, #375) show how often interactions between distant parts have already produced defects, and findings 15-17 here are of the same kind.

**Failure scenario.** A change to one concern (for example flow control) has to be made in three files and reasoned against locks declared in a fourth; nothing stops a send-path method from touching read-loop-owned state. Review and fix rounds keep producing sibling bugs (CLAUDE.md section 7.4 notes this), and the semantic parts cannot be unit-tested without a full connection.

## Suggested fix
Extract cohesive collaborators with explicit owners: a header-block assembler (CONTINUATION accumulation and limits), a static response-head validator shared with HTTP/1.1, a receive-window controller, the admission queue (already self-contained) and the PING liveness probe; keep Http2Connection as the frame router. Update architecture.md.

## Acceptance criteria

title: [HTTP/2] InitializeAsync awaits the server SETTINGS ACK before dispatch, adding a round trip to every new connection
body:
## Summary
Http2Connection.InitializeAsync writes the preface and SETTINGS, then awaits the peer's SETTINGS ACK before Http2ConnectionManager publishes the connection and the transport dispatches the first request. RFC 9113 section 3.4 allows the client to send frames right after its preface. Every new HTTP/2 connection therefore pays one extra round trip, which matters most on high-latency mobile links and after every GOAWAY or network change.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.cs:265`

## Problem
InitializeAsync writes the preface and SETTINGS, starts the read loop and then awaits _settingsAckSource (Http2Connection.cs:248-267); Http2ConnectionManager.GetOrCreateSlowAsync awaits InitializeAsync before it returns the connection (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:333), and the transport dispatches only afterwards (RawSocketTransport.cs:629-642). The ACK can only arrive one full round trip after the client SETTINGS were sent. RFC 9113 Section 3.4 lets the client send frames immediately after its preface; the defaults for the peer's settings apply until its SETTINGS arrive (the admission and window code already handles later changes).

**Failure scenario.** On a 150 ms RTT mobile link the first request on each new connection takes TCP + TLS 1.3 + one extra RTT + the request itself: about 600 ms instead of 450 ms; the same cost recurs after every GOAWAY, idle close or network change.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 3.4

## Suggested fix
Publish the connection and allow dispatch once preface and SETTINGS are written and the read loop runs; keep the SETTINGS ACK deadline as a background liveness check that fails the connection (and its streams as retryable) when it expires.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The connection is published and the first request may be dispatched once the preface and SETTINGS are written and the read loop is running, without waiting for the SETTINGS ACK.
- [ ] The SETTINGS ACK deadline remains as a background liveness check; when it expires the connection fails and its open streams fail as retryable.
- [ ] Peer settings that arrive later (including lower initial window or max concurrent streams) are applied correctly to streams already opened.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix, showing that a request is written before the server's SETTINGS ACK is sent, and that a missing ACK still fails the connection.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-10` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. Http2Connection.InitializeAsync writes preface + SETTINGS, starts the read loop and awaits _settingsAckSource (Http2Connection.cs:232-266); the source is completed with success only by an inbound SETTINGS frame carrying ACK (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:829-836), not by the server preface. Http2ConnectionManager.GetOrCreateSlowAsync awaits InitializeAsync before TryPublish/return (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:333-351) and RawSocketTransport dispatches only after GetOrCreateAsync returns (RawSocketTransport.cs:629-642). The ACK needs the server to have read the client SETTINGS, so HEADERS leave one RTT later than RFC 9113 Section 3.4 allows. No comment or issue documents this as a deliberate trade-off (rg for 'SETTINGS ACK' in Http2/, agent guides and Documentation~ finds only the timeout constant and the wait itself). No guard refutes it; the admission code already handles later SETTINGS (remote MaxConcurrentStreams defaults to int.MaxValue, Http2Settings.cs:15; limit re-checked at Http2Connection.cs:351). Cost is per new connection, not per request.

Related: #406.

title: [HTTP/2] content-length is caller-owned and never generated on HTTP/2, but transport-owned on HTTP/1.1
body:
## Summary
On HTTP/1.1 the serializer owns content-length and derives it from the body, while the HTTP/2 request head in Http2Connection copies the caller's value and never generates one. The two protocols can therefore send different framing metadata for the same request, and a caller-supplied value that disagrees with the body is forwarded on HTTP/2. Callers see protocol-dependent behaviour they cannot choose.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.cs:379`

## Problem
HTTP/1.1: Http11RequestSerializer skips caller Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding (IsFramingHeader, Http11RequestSerializer.cs:320-326, 509-513) and writes Content-Length from the body's known length (lines 339-348). HTTP/2: the header loop (Http2Connection.cs:379-402) only drops IsHttp2ForbiddenHeader names (Http2Connection.Send.cs:560-568: connection, transfer-encoding, keep-alive, proxy-connection, upgrade, host), so a caller-supplied content-length is forwarded verbatim without being compared with the body, and nothing adds content-length for a buffered or known-length body (no 'content-length' on the request side anywhere in Runtime/Transport/Http2; no Core code sets the request header either). No HTTP/2 test covers request content-length.

**Failure scenario.** The same UHttpRequest behaves differently depending on ALPN, which the caller does not choose: (a) a request carrying a stale or wrong Content-Length header works on HTTP/1.1 (replaced) but is malformed on HTTP/2 and reset by the server with PROTOCOL_ERROR (RFC 9113 Section 8.1.1); (b) every POST/PUT with a known-length body goes out on HTTP/2 without content-length, against the RFC 9110 Section 8.6 SHOULD, so origins, WAFs or frameworks that require a length answer 411 or treat the upload as unbounded only on the HTTP/2 path.

## Spec reference
RFC 9110 Section 8.6; RFC 9113 Section 8.1.1

## Suggested fix
Build the request head in one place for both protocols: treat content-length as transport-owned on HTTP/2 too (drop the caller's value, emit the body's known length), sharing the body-mode decision the HTTP/1.1 serializer already makes.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] On HTTP/2 the caller's content-length header is dropped and the transport emits content-length from the body's known length when the length is known (RFC 9113 section 8.6).
- [ ] HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 share one body-mode decision for content-length, so both protocols produce the same value for the same request.
- [ ] A caller-supplied content-length that differs from the body length is never sent on either protocol.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix covering known-length body, unknown-length body and a mismatching caller header on HTTP/2.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-design-09` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: code-smell.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. HTTP/1.1 skips caller Content-Length/Transfer-Encoding and writes its own from the body mode (Http11RequestSerializer.cs:320-348, 509-513). The HTTP/2 header loop drops only IsHttp2ForbiddenHeader names (Http2Connection.cs:379-402; Send.cs:560-568: connection, transfer-encoding, keep-alive, proxy-connection, upgrade, host), so a caller content-length is lower-cased and forwarded verbatim, and nothing generates one: rg for content-length in Runtime shows no request-side producer in Http2/ or Core (only the response checks in ReadLoop.cs and RedirectInterceptor.cs:205 removing it). SendStreamingDataAsync does know the length (session.ContentLength, Send.cs:262) but only uses it to bound the read. No HTTP/2 test covers a request content-length. Part (a) (stale caller value becomes a malformed request, RFC 9113 Section 8.1.1) is a protocol-dependent behaviour difference; part (b) (missing content-length, RFC 9110 Section 8.6 SHOULD) is legal on HTTP/2 and its interop impact depends on the origin.

title: [HTTP/2] Request-body failure after response HEADERS resets the stream but never faults the response body source
body:
## Summary
When the request body throws after the response has started, the Http2Connection dispatch catch sends RST_STREAM but does not fail the stream, so the response body source is never faulted. The reader waits forever and the pooled buffers and the connection's buffered-byte count held by the body source are never released. This leaks pooled memory and hangs the caller reading the response.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Connection.cs:487`

## Problem
DispatchAsync catch (Http2Connection.cs:481-512): for an upload exception with HEADERS sent it calls stream.AbortRequestBody() and ResetStreamIfActiveAsync(CANCEL) only, then rethrows; the finally (513-525) disposes the cancellation registration and releases the dispatch reference. Nothing calls stream.Fail/FaultResponseBody, unlike every other path that removes a stream (ReadLoop.cs:226, 242, 265, 313, 383, 398, 548; Lifecycle.cs:194, 218). The stream is now out of _activeStreams, so later RST_STREAM/DATA, FailAllStreams (Lifecycle.cs:569-573), ScanForStalledStreams (Lifecycle.cs:473) and the request deadline (registration disposed) can no longer reach the body source: it stays TerminalStateActive. Queued chunks stay rented from ByteArrayPool and _connectionBufferedBytes is never decremented (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:319, released only in ReadAsync/cleanup).

**Failure scenario.** Streaming POST whose response starts before the upload ends (bidirectional endpoint, early 200); the caller's request-body stream throws IOException (or the body ends before its declared Content-Length, Send.cs:282, or the trailer provider throws). The dispatch fails with the upload error, RST_STREAM(CANCEL) is sent, and the consumer's pending or next ReadAsync on the response body never completes (no data, no fault, no timeout). Each such stream keeps up to its window of DATA in pooled buffers and counts against MaxConnectionBufferedBytes; enough of them stop connection-level WINDOW_UPDATEs (Lifecycle.cs:359).

## Suggested fix
In the dispatch catch, fail the stream (stream.Fail with the mapped error) before or together with the reset when the response has started, so the body source is faulted and cleaned up like on every other reset path; add a test with a throwing request body after response HEADERS.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] When a request-body failure occurs after the response started, the stream is failed with the mapped error so the response body source is faulted and its buffers and buffered-byte accounting are released.
- [ ] The reader of the response body receives a UHttpException instead of waiting indefinitely.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix with a throwing request body after response HEADERS, asserting the reader faults and buffered bytes return to zero.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-02` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: resource-management.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: DispatchAsync catch (Http2Connection.cs:487-501): for an upload failure with HEADERS sent and ct not cancelled it calls stream.AbortRequestBody() and ResetStreamIfActiveAsync(CANCEL) (which removes the stream, Lifecycle.cs:172-179) and rethrows; nothing calls stream.Fail/FaultResponseBody. With the stream out of _activeStreams, FailAllStreams (Lifecycle.cs:569-573), ScanForStalledStreams (473) and the read loop cannot reach the body source, and the finally disposes the request-token registration (523), so the source stays TerminalStateActive: a pending or later ReadAsync waits on _queue.ReadAsync forever unless the reader's own token fires, queued chunks stay rented and _connectionBufferedBytes is not released (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:311-319), and the stream object never returns to the pool. Reachable sources of the exception: request-body stream read error, short body vs Content-Length (Send.cs:281-284), trailer provider/validation throwing. In the buffered path the collector still gets OnResponseError from the transport, but its read loop stays parked; in the streaming path the safety wrapper drops that callback and the caller's body read hangs with no error. Needs a response that starts before the upload ends, hence medium. Connection-level write failures are not affected (FailAllStreams runs while the stream is still active).

title: [HTTP/2] No idle timeout for connections and reuse probe off by default, so first request after a silent NAT drop stalls
body:
## Summary
Http2ConnectionManager does not apply ConnectionPoolOptions.ConnectionIdleTimeout to HTTP/2 connections and the reuse probe is disabled by default. After a silent NAT drop or app resume, the first request on the dead connection waits for the request deadline or up to PingInterval + PingTimeout before failing over. Mobile users hit this after backgrounding.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2ConnectionManager.cs:184`

## Problem
SelectConnection returns any connection whose read loop still runs (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:184-216; Http2Connection.cs:140-151); nothing closes a connection that has been idle. Http2Options.ReuseProbeIdleThreshold defaults to zero (Http2Options.cs:21, 205-206) with the argument that PINGs on idle connections cost battery, but this probe only runs when a request is about to use the radio anyway. Liveness PINGs run on a free-running 30 s timer and only while streams are open (Liveness.cs:42-51, 75), so a request on a black-holed connection is detected after up to 30 s + 10 s, later than the default 30 s/45 s request timeout (UHttpRequest.cs:147, PlatformConfig.cs:21-26). For HTTP/1.1 the project already uses a 45 s idle timeout on mobile for exactly this reason (PlatformConfig.cs:31-35, #47); the HTTP/2 manager has no equivalent. A connection failure before the response is replayed only for idempotent methods (RawSocketTransport.cs:217-219).

**Failure scenario.** Android or iOS on a carrier NAT, app idle for a few minutes or resumed from background: the next https request reuses the pooled HTTP/2 connection, HEADERS go into the kernel buffer, no answer comes, and the request ends with Timeout (or, with a longer timeout, with a network error after the PING cycle); a POST is not replayed. Needs a device or a network emulator that drops the flow silently to confirm the timing.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 6.7

## Suggested fix
Apply ConnectionPoolOptions.ConnectionIdleTimeout to HTTP/2 connections with no open streams (close with GOAWAY and retire them), and enable the reuse probe by default on mobile with a threshold below typical NAT timeouts, or start the first liveness PING relative to the request start.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] HTTP/2 connections with no open streams are closed (GOAWAY) and retired after ConnectionIdleTimeout.
- [ ] A liveness probe before reuse is enabled by default on mobile with a threshold below typical NAT timeouts, or the first liveness PING is measured from the request start.
- [ ] The first request after a silent drop fails over to a fresh connection within the probe timeout instead of the full deadline.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix using a virtual clock, plus validated on a device and recorded.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-12` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: platform-compat.

Verification: Plausible: the code is as described; the outcome depends on runtime, device or peer behaviour that a static review cannot settle.

Verifier note: Code is as described: Http2ConnectionManager has no idle timeout (no 'idle' logic in the file; SelectConnection returns any connection with AcceptsNewStreams, lines 184-216); ReuseProbeIdleThreshold defaults to TimeSpan.Zero (Http2Options.cs:21, 205-217) so the probe at Http2Connection.cs:330 is skipped; liveness PINGs run on a free-running Task.Delay(_pingInterval) loop and only when _activeStreams is non-empty (Liveness.cs:42-51, 75), so detection on a black-holed connection takes up to PingInterval + PingTimeout (30 s + 10 s) against a default 30 s/45 s request timeout (UHttpRequest.cs:147, PlatformConfig.cs:19-27). No SO_KEEPALIVE is set (platform.md:68; no keepalive socket option in Runtime/Transport/Tcp). HTTP/1.1 has both a 45 s mobile idle timeout and a 10 s reused-connection first-byte timeout (PlatformConfig.cs:36, 44); HTTP/2 has neither. The default-off probe is a documented decision (#238 closed, Transport.md:69), but its stated reason (idle PINGs cost battery) does not apply to a probe sent only when a request is about to go out. The actual failure depends on NAT/radio behaviour and cannot be settled statically; needs-device-validation.

title: [HTTP/2] Http2ConnectionManager.Dispose does not fence an in-flight init: connection leaks and disposed semaphores break waiters
body:
## Summary
Http2ConnectionManager.Dispose disposes the per-key init semaphores while an InitializeAsync may be running or waiting. The new connection is then published into the disposed manager and leaks, and holders and waiters of the disposed semaphores throw ObjectDisposedException. Callers can also get a synchronous throw instead of a faulted task.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2ConnectionManager.cs:465`

## Problem
GetOrCreateAsync checks _disposed only on entry (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:227, 258). GetOrCreateSlowAsync then awaits initLock.WaitAsync and newConnection.InitializeAsync (lines 307, 333; InitializeAsync waits at least one round trip for the SETTINGS ACK) and calls TryPublish (lines 339, 380-408), which never looks at _disposed. Dispose (lines 465-489) disposes the connections published so far, then disposes every SemaphoreSlim in _initLocks (lines 483-487). When Dispose runs during that await: TryPublish adds the connection to _connections of a disposed manager (published = true), the finally block's initLock.Release() throws ObjectDisposedException (line 355), and the catch at lines 364-373 skips cleanup because published is true. The codebase documents the semaphore hazard itself for _writeLock (Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:653-658: 'SemaphoreSlim.Dispose never completes async waiters, and a Release after Dispose throws'). RawSocketTransport.Dispose (RawSocketTransport.cs:2425-2432) does not cancel in-flight requests. The disposed path also throws ObjectDisposedException synchronously from a ValueTask-returning method (lines 227-231).

**Failure scenario.** UHttpClient/transport is disposed (scene unload, shutdown) while the first request to an h2 origin is still initialising its connection: the request fails with ObjectDisposedException mapped to UHttpErrorType.Unknown, and the initialised Http2Connection (socket, TLS state, read loop, keep-alive and maintenance loops) stays alive unowned until the server closes it; it is never Dispose()d, so its stream is only released by finalisation. A second request queued on the same init lock is never granted and ends only when its own token fires. With Enter Play Mode without domain reload the leaked loops survive into the next session.

## Suggested fix
Do not dispose the init semaphores (or drain them first); re-check _disposed after InitializeAsync and again after TryPublish and dispose/unpublish the connection when the manager was disposed meanwhile; return a faulted ValueTask (or a UHttpException) instead of throwing synchronously.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] After Dispose, a connection whose init completes is disposed and never published; the manager holds no live connections.
- [ ] Init semaphores are not disposed while holders or waiters exist; waiters observe a UHttpException or cancellation rather than ObjectDisposedException.
- [ ] Requests on a disposed manager return a faulted ValueTask rather than throwing synchronously.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix that disposes the manager during InitializeAsync and asserts no leaked connection.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-design-15` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: best-practices.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. GetOrCreateAsync checks _disposed only on entry (Http2ConnectionManager.cs:227, 258). GetOrCreateSlowAsync then awaits initLock.WaitAsync and InitializeAsync (307, 333; at least one RTT, up to the 5 s ACK timeout) and calls TryPublish (339, 380-408), which never reads _disposed, unlike RemoveExactAndRetire (510, 525-527). If Dispose (465-489) runs in that window it clears _connections and disposes the init semaphores; TryPublish then TryAdds into the cleared dictionary, published = true, initLock.Release() in the finally (355) throws ObjectDisposedException on the disposed SemaphoreSlim, and the catch (364-373) skips cleanup because published is true. The transferred TLS stream is not owned by the pool any more (lease.TransferOwnership, RawSocketTransport.cs:625), and neither RawSocketTransport.Dispose (2425-2432) nor UHttpClient.DisposeOwnedComponents (UHttpClient.cs:590-606) cancels in-flight requests, so nothing closes the connection: its read loop and maintenance loop run until the peer closes it, and after that it is never Dispose()d (see http2-runtime-11). Waiters queued on the disposed semaphore are not completed by Dispose and end only at their own token. The synchronous ObjectDisposedException from a ValueTask-returning method (227-231) is real but harmless to the awaiting caller. Narrow window (shutdown during a first request's HTTP/2 init) and a bounded leak, hence medium at most.

Also reported as `http2-runtime-13` (merged into this issue).

title: [HTTP/2] Http2FrameCodec write-progress timestamp is a long accessed via Volatile on 32-bit IL2CPP
body:
## Summary
Http2FrameCodec reads and writes the long field _writeProgressTimestamp with Volatile.Read/Write, while neighbouring 64-bit fields use Interlocked. On 32-bit IL2CPP, 64-bit Volatile access is not guaranteed atomic, so a torn read can report a false send stall and fail a healthy connection.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2FrameCodec.cs:73`

## Problem
_writeProgressTimestamp (Http2FrameCodec.cs:58) is written by the frame writer with Volatile.Write (81, 241) and read by the maintenance loop with Volatile.Read (73). Elsewhere the slice states that longs are accessed through Interlocked only because of 32-bit IL2CPP (Liveness.cs:14, 29-30; Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:79). The value toggles between 0 and a timestamp several times per frame. A reader that sees the low word of a new timestamp with the old zero high word gets a small non-zero value, and IsWriteStalled then reports elapsed time since boot (73-75), which leads to FailAllStreams and Dispose (Lifecycle.cs:499-511).

**Failure scenario.** On an ARMv7 IL2CPP player under sustained traffic the maintenance tick lands between the two halves of a write to the field and a healthy connection is failed with 'send stalled'. Whether IL2CPP's Volatile.Read(ref long) is atomic on 32-bit targets must be checked in the generated code or on a device.

## Suggested fix
Use Interlocked.Read/Interlocked.Exchange for _writeProgressTimestamp, as the neighbouring long fields do.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] _writeProgressTimestamp is read and written with Interlocked.Read and Interlocked.Exchange.
- [ ] No other 64-bit field in Runtime/Transport/Http2 is accessed with Volatile.
- [ ] A test or analyzer check guards the pattern in Tests/Runtime/Transport/.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-25` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: platform-compat.

Verification: Not independently verified: low-severity findings were not sent to a second reviewer. Re-trace it in the code before fixing.

title: [HTTP/2] Every frame is written as separate header and payload writes, costing two TLS records and two sends
body:
## Summary
Http2FrameCodec writes each frame's 9-byte header and its payload as two stream writes. Each frame therefore costs two TLS records, two send syscalls and, with TCP_NODELAY, two segments. This inflates overhead on all HTTP/2 traffic and contributes to the throughput gap in #406.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2FrameCodec.cs:221`

## Problem
WriteFrameAsync writes the 9-byte header with one _stream.WriteAsync (Http2FrameCodec.cs:221), the payload with another per 16 KB slice (229) and then FlushAsync (236). The stream is the TLS stream directly (no coalescing wrapper: Http2Connection.cs:175, RawSocketTransport.cs:629-630); SslStream and BouncyCastleTlsStream emit one record per write, and sockets are created with NoDelay = true (HappyEyeballsConnector.cs:491). InitializeAsync adds three more writes for preface and SETTINGS (Http2Connection.cs:232-243). A 13-byte WINDOW_UPDATE or RST_STREAM becomes two records of 9 and 4 plaintext bytes.

**Failure scenario.** A small POST leaves as four TLS records and four packets (HEADERS header, header block, DATA header, body) instead of one; a 16 KB DATA frame costs an extra record, syscall and packet for its 9-byte header, on upload and for every control frame on download.

## Suggested fix
Serialize header and payload into one pooled buffer for small frames (control frames, HEADERS, small DATA) and issue a single write; for large DATA at least coalesce the header with the first slice, and write HEADERS plus the first DATA frame of a request under one lock hold.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Small frames (control frames, HEADERS, small DATA) are serialized into one pooled buffer and written with a single stream write.
- [ ] For large DATA frames the header is coalesced with the first payload slice; HEADERS and the first DATA frame of a request go out under one lock hold.
- [ ] Measured target: one stream write per small frame, and one TLS record per frame on the send path.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix using a counting stream that asserts the number of writes per frame.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-08` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Covered by #406 (suspect 'Small DATA frame or TLS record sizes on the send path'). WriteFrameAsync issues a separate _stream.WriteAsync for the 9-byte header (Http2FrameCodec.cs:221), one per 16 KB payload slice (229) and a flush (236); the codec wraps the TLS stream directly (Http2Connection.cs:172-175, no BufferedStream/coalescing type under Runtime/Transport), BouncyCastleTlsStream encrypts and drains per write call (BouncyCastleTlsStream.cs:205-244) as SslStream does, and sockets are NoDelay (HappyEyeballsConnector.cs:491). Preface and SETTINGS are separate writes too (Http2Connection.cs:232-243). So every frame is at least two TLS records and two sends; a WINDOW_UPDATE/RST_STREAM is a 9-byte and a 4-byte record.

Related: #406, [[R11-http2-runtime-09]], [[R11-http2-runtime-07]].

title: [HTTP/2] ConfigureAwait(false) is missing on several awaits in Http2FrameCodec
body:
## Summary
Several awaits in Http2FrameCodec do not use ConfigureAwait(false), against the project's own rule for library code. Continuations can resume on the Unity synchronization context, which risks stalls and deadlocks in transport code.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2FrameCodec.cs:260`

## Problem
Awaits without ConfigureAwait(false): Http2FrameCodec.cs:90, 117, 136, 250, 252, 260 (ReadFrameAsync, ReadFrameLeaseAsync, WritePrefaceAsync, ReadExactAsync); Http2Connection.cs:232, 236 (InitializeAsync preface and SETTINGS writes); Http2ConnectionManager.cs:307, 333 (init lock wait, InitializeAsync); Http2Connection.Send.cs:189 (_writeLock.WaitAsync in the DATA loop); Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:39, 73, 76, 77, 79, 81, 102, 112, 1203. platform.md states 'use ConfigureAwait(false) everywhere else' and that library code never relies on the caller's SynchronizationContext.

**Failure scenario.** The read loop runs under Task.Run and the production call chain has usually left the Unity context before these awaits, so today the effect is nil. A caller that reaches GetOrCreateAsync/InitializeAsync or the DATA loop with UnitySynchronizationContext still current (tests, a future refactor, a synchronously completing earlier await) gets connection setup and every DATA frame continuation posted to the main thread, where a blocked or paused main thread stalls the connection (#245).

## Suggested fix
Add ConfigureAwait(false) at the listed sites; consider the analyzer rule (CA2007) for the Transport assembly so new sites fail the build.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] ConfigureAwait(false) is added at every listed await site in Runtime/Transport/Http2.
- [ ] The CA2007 analyzer rule is enabled for the Transport assembly so new sites fail the build, with no baselined warnings.
- [ ] The change is verified by Tools~/ci/check.sh with no new analyzer warnings.

title: [HTTP/2] End of response body is signalled by a thrown InvalidOperationException, one per completed body
body:
## Summary
Http2ResponseBodySource relies on SingleReaderChannel throwing InvalidOperationException to signal the end of the body. One exception is thrown and caught for every response body read to completion, which is costly on IL2CPP and adds allocations on a hot path.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:217`

## Problem
At EOF ReadAsync finds no chunk and calls _queue.ReadAsync; a completed empty channel returns Task.FromException(new InvalidOperationException('Channel completed.')) (SingleReaderChannel.cs:116-120), and a reader that was already pending is completed with SetException of the same type (SingleReaderChannel.cs:157-169). ReadAsync turns it into 'return 0' with an exception filter (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:212-220). Only bodies taken through TryDetachBufferedBody avoid it.

**Failure scenario.** Every HTTP/2 response whose body is read until 0 throws and catches one exception: an allocation of the exception, a faulted task and stack capture, and on IL2CPP a C++ exception unwind costing tens of microseconds per request; in the Editor it also trips first-chance exception breakpoints on every request.

## Suggested fix
Give SingleReaderChannel a non-throwing completion signal (TryRead plus a completed flag, or ReadAsync returning a (bool, T) result) and return 0 from ReadAsync without an exception.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] SingleReaderChannel exposes a non-throwing completion signal and ReadAsync returns 0 at end of body without an exception.
- [ ] Measured target: zero exceptions thrown per response body read to completion.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix asserting no first-chance exception on normal completion and unchanged error propagation on failure.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-16` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: low. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Traced. At EOF Http2ResponseBodySource.ReadAsync finds no chunk, calls _queue.ReadAsync and turns the resulting InvalidOperationException into 'return 0' with an exception filter (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:211-220); the channel produces it either as Task.FromException on a completed empty channel (SingleReaderChannel.cs:116-120) or via SetException on the pending reader (SingleReaderChannel.cs:157-169). There is no completed-state check before the channel read. It also hits the default buffered path whenever the body is not already complete when collection starts, because TryDetachBufferedBody requires TerminalStateCompleted (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:96-102) and ResponseCollectorHandler then reads until 0 (ResponseCollectorHandler.cs:173-187). Severity lowered: one throw/catch per response body (not per read), no correctness effect, and small next to the network cost of the request; the debugger first-chance noise is real.

title: [HTTP/2] Receive buffering counts payload bytes only: a flood of 1-byte DATA frames costs a pooled array and queue slot per byte
body:
## Summary
Http2ResponseBodySource bounds receive buffering by payload bytes only. A peer sending many 1-byte DATA frames makes the client rent one pooled array and a queue slot per byte, so memory use is a large multiple of the configured limit. A malicious server can amplify memory and CPU cost cheaply.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:293`

## Problem
TryEnqueueData reserves `length` against _bufferCapacity, then rents one buffer per DATA frame and enqueues a 16-byte Http2ResponseBodyChunk (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:281-334, 500-515); the channel capacity is int.MaxValue (line 64). Flow control bounds the unread bytes per stream to the stream window (65535 by default) and per connection to roughly MaxConnectionBufferedBytes (8 MiB) plus the 1 MiB window target (Http2Connection.Lifecycle.cs:353-390), but both count flow-controlled bytes, not objects. ArrayPool's smallest bucket is 16 bytes, so each 1-byte frame holds ~40 bytes of array plus the queue slot.

**Failure scenario.** A hostile server sends a response as 1-byte DATA frames to a consumer that reads slower than the network (or is paused): one stream holds up to 65535 chunks (~3.5 MB instead of 64 KB); with many concurrent slow streams the connection-level bound of ~9 MiB of payload translates into ~500 MB of small arrays and segments until the 60 s stall timeout aborts the bodies - a ~50x amplification of the documented buffer limits on a mobile device.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 10.5

## Suggested fix
Coalesce small DATA payloads into the tail chunk (append into a larger rented buffer while it has room) or charge a fixed per-chunk overhead against the buffer capacity; optionally reset a stream that delivers an excessive number of tiny frames (ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Small DATA payloads are coalesced into the tail chunk, or a fixed per-chunk overhead is charged against the buffer capacity.
- [ ] A stream delivering an excessive number of tiny frames is reset with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM.
- [ ] Pooled arrays and queue slots for a flood of N 1-byte frames stay below a stated bound that is asserted in the test.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix with a 1-byte DATA flood.

## Context

title: [HTTP/2] Each DATA payload is copied into a second pooled buffer and each frame allocates a lease, frame object and tasks
body:
## Summary
Http2ResponseBodySource copies every DATA payload from the leased frame buffer into a second pooled buffer, and each frame allocates a lease, an Http2Frame object and task objects, with no read buffering. This adds copies and allocations per frame on the download hot path and contributes to the throughput gap in #406.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:296`

## Problem
ReadFrameLeaseAsync reads the 9-byte header and the payload with separate ReadAsync calls on the TLS stream (Http2FrameCodec.cs:117, 136, 260) and allocates an Http2Frame, an Http2FrameReadLease and a Task<Http2FrameReadLease> per frame (151-158). TryEnqueueData then rents another buffer and BlockCopies the payload (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:296-299) although the read loop already owns an exclusively leased buffer of the right size; the consumer copies a third time into its destination (546-547).

**Failure scenario.** A 100 MiB download performs 6400 extra 16 KB copies and pool rent/return pairs and at least three small allocations per frame on the read loop, part of the per-frame cost behind #406.

## Suggested fix
Transfer ownership of the frame's rented payload buffer to the body source (offset/length for padded frames) instead of copying; reuse one Http2Frame/lease per connection (struct or reset); read through a 16-64 KB buffered reader so header and payload usually come from one stream read.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The frame's rented payload buffer is handed to the body source (with offset and length for padded frames) instead of being copied.
- [ ] One Http2Frame or lease is reused per connection, and header plus payload usually come from one buffered stream read.
- [ ] Measured target: zero payload copies and zero per-frame heap allocations on the steady-state DATA path, asserted by the allocation gate.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix covering ownership transfer and exactly-once buffer return.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-09` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Covered by #406 (suspect 'Per-DATA-frame overhead in the read loop or the body queue'). ReadFrameLeaseAsync reads header and payload with separate ReadExactAsync calls on the unbuffered TLS stream (Http2FrameCodec.cs:117, 136, 258-266) and allocates an Http2Frame (class, Http2Frame.cs:74), an Http2FrameReadLease (class, Http2FrameCodec.cs:13) and the Task<Http2FrameReadLease> per frame (114, 151-158). TryEnqueueData rents a second buffer and BlockCopies the payload out of the already exclusively leased frame buffer (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:296-299); the consumer copies again in TryReadCurrentChunk (546-547). Not a correctness defect; per-frame copy and allocation cost on the download hot path.

Related: #120, #406, [[R11-http2-runtime-08]], [[R11-http2-runtime-07]].

title: [HTTP/2] Body reader sends and awaits one stream WINDOW_UPDATE per DATA frame; allocation gate bypasses this path
body:
## Summary
Http2ResponseBodySource sends one stream WINDOW_UPDATE for each consumed DATA frame and awaits that write before returning data to the caller. This adds a write and a round of latency per frame and slows streaming downloads, while the existing allocation gate test does not exercise the path. This is part of the throughput gap in #406.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:413`

## Problem
ReadAsync awaits CompleteDetachedChunkAsync for every finished chunk, one chunk per DATA frame (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:200-203, 296-305, 413). Each update goes through OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync -> SendWindowUpdateAsync -> SendFrameWithPooledPayloadAsync -> WriteFrameLockedAsync -> Http2FrameCodec.WriteFrameAsync: seven nested async methods that box when the write is asynchronous, a closure plus delegate for the payload filler (Lifecycle.cs:41-47), a pool rent, a _writeLock acquisition and three stream calls (header, payload, flush). The consumer's read therefore waits behind whatever holds _writeLock (for example another stream's 16 KB upload write). StreamingAllocationGateTests.cs:417-423 enqueues chunks with flowControlledLength: 0, so OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync returns early (Lifecycle.cs:297) and the 0 B/read budget does not measure the real path.

**Failure scenario.** A 100 MiB download at 16 KB frames issues 6400 WINDOW_UPDATE frames (12800 TLS records and send syscalls, see finding 08) and roughly 1 KB of garbage each on Mono/IL2CPP; reads of already-buffered data are delayed by concurrent uploads on the same connection.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 6.9

## Suggested fix
Batch stream credit: accumulate consumed bytes and send WINDOW_UPDATE when they reach a fraction (for example half) of the window; hand the frame to a non-awaited, owned control-frame queue instead of awaiting it in ReadAsync; extend the allocation gate with a non-zero flow-controlled length.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Consumed bytes are accumulated and WINDOW_UPDATE is sent when they reach a fraction (for example half) of the window.
- [ ] The WINDOW_UPDATE write is queued to an owned control-frame queue and not awaited inside ReadAsync.
- [ ] The allocation gate is extended with a non-zero flow-controlled length; measured target: at most one WINDOW_UPDATE per half window.
- [ ] Add a deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ that fails before the fix counting WINDOW_UPDATE frames for a multi-frame body.

## Context
Source: 2026-11 full-library review, finding `http2-runtime-07` in `Development~/docs/review-2026-11/http2.md`, reviewed at commit `0e0f1bc`. Severity: medium. Angle: performance.

Verification: Confirmed: a second reviewer re-traced the failure scenario in the code.

Verifier note: Covered by #406 (suspect 'WINDOW_UPDATE ... in too-small increments' / per-DATA-frame overhead). Code as described: one chunk per DATA frame (Http2ResponseBodySource.cs:296-305), and ReadAsync awaits CompleteDetachedChunkAsync for each finished chunk before returning (200-203, 413) -> OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync -> SendWindowUpdateAsync, whose lambda captures `increment` (closure + delegate per call, Lifecycle.cs:35-48) -> _writeLock wait -> WriteFrameAsync with header write, payload write and flush (Http2FrameCodec.cs:221-236). The reader therefore queues behind any other writer holding _writeLock. New relative to the issue: the allocation gate does not exercise this path, StreamingAllocationGateTests.cs:417-423 enqueues with flowControlledLength: 0 so OnStreamChunkConsumedAsync returns at Lifecycle.cs:297.

Related: #406, [[R11-http2-runtime-09]], [[R11-http2-runtime-08]].

title: [HTTP/2] A server SETTINGS frame with ENABLE_PUSH=1 is acknowledged instead of rejected with PROTOCOL_ERROR
body:
## Summary
Http2Settings.Apply rejects only ENABLE_PUSH values above 1, and the connection applies the remote settings unchanged. RFC 9113 section 6.5.2 requires a client to treat a server SETTINGS frame with ENABLE_PUSH set to 1 as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR. The gap is a conformance issue only, because the client never accepts pushes.

## Location
- `Runtime/Transport/Http2/Http2Settings.cs:53`

## Problem
Http2Settings.Apply rejects only value > 1 for EnablePush (Http2Settings.cs:53-58); HandleSettingsFrameAsync applies it to _remoteSettings unchanged (Http2Connection.ReadLoop.cs:850-852). RFC 9113 6.5.2: 'A client MUST treat receipt of a SETTINGS frame with SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH set to 1 as a connection error of type PROTOCOL_ERROR.'

**Failure scenario.** Server sends SETTINGS {ENABLE_PUSH: 1}; the client ACKs it instead of sending GOAWAY(PROTOCOL_ERROR). No further effect (the client never pushes), so this is a conformance gap only.

## Spec reference
RFC 9113 Section 6.5.2

## Suggested fix
In the remote-settings path, treat ENABLE_PUSH != 0 as a connection PROTOCOL_ERROR (keep the 0/1 rule for the local settings object).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A server SETTINGS frame with SETTINGS_ENABLE_PUSH=1 makes the client send GOAWAY(PROTOCOL_ERROR) and fail the connection with a UHttpException
- [ ] The 0/1 rule for the local settings object is unchanged
- [ ] A deterministic NUnit regression test under Tests/Runtime/Transport/ fails before the fix and passes after it

## Context
